Would You Have Paid New CLA Money for this V8-Powered Mercedes G-Class?
14 photos
Photo: Cars&Bids
Yeah, it’s not exactly part of the new generation Mercedes G-Wagen , but truth be told, the average Joe will likely not be able to tell the difference, at least when it comes to the exterior, because the cockpit does look old.
This machine is a 2015 model year car that is said to have had a single owner in the papers until 2026. The seller reportedly picked it up in July 2026, and after adding some 5,000 miles (8,000 km), they put it up for grabs, accepting $53,000. Is that a good deal? Well, this model usually sells from roughly $35,000 to over $60,000, and the selling price equals a brand-new CLA, as mentioned in the title.
But what model is it exactly? That would be a G 550 , meaning that it packs a V8 engine. The M273 unit that breathes air from behind the familiar-looking grille has a 5.5-liter displacement, and was good for 382 hp (387 ps/285 kW) and 391 lb-ft (530 Nm) of torque when the truck was new, enabling 0-62 mph (100 kph) in roughly six seconds. This previous generation Mercedes-Benz G-Class features a seven-speed automatic transmission, a two-speed transfer case, and four-wheel drive.
The vehicle has a black-on-black look, complemented by some chrome accents on the outside. The Exterior Stainless Steel Package is on deck, just like the Parking Package. A sport exhaust system, 18-inch wheels, a power sunroof, Designo black leather upholstery, adaptive cruise control, and a premium sound system from Harman Kardon are also included.
Photo: Cars&Bids An internal crack in the left headlight was mentioned by the owner as being a flaw, and other issues include some corrosion on the underbody components, scuffs on the cargo area sill plate, and wear on certain interior surfaces and touch points.
The A/C refrigerant was recharged, and the engine oil and filter were changed in August 2025, and more than a year before, the starter was replaced. In December 2023, when this older Mercedes G-Wagen had 61,149 miles (98,410 km), the engine oil and filter, and the brake fluid were changed, and the serpentine belt and idler puller were replaced. The thermostat was replaced in May 2022, at 48,088 miles (77,390 km), and the battery was replaced in January that same year.
At the time of cataloging, the German premium truck from the previous generation had 82,400 miles (132,600 km) on the odo. It has a clean South Carolina title, has never been involved in an accident, and has no mileage discrepancies. In addition to the vehicle, the new owner will get two keys and the tool kit, because this machine comes from a long-gone era.
If you were shopping for a previous-gen G-Wagen and came across this one listed for $53,000, would you have bought it? Those who want to see more of it can do so here on Cars&Bids.

Container shipping spot rates from Asia to the United States declined in the latest week as offered capacity increased on routes to both U.S. coasts, according to Xeneta’s latest market update.
Average rates to the U.S. West Coast fell 1.7% to $8,203 per 40-foot container (FEU), while rates to the U.S. East Coast dropped 1.9% to $10,901 per FEU, for the week ending Nov. 19.
The declines accompanied a substantial expansion in offered capacity. Based on four-week rolling averages, capacity from the Far East to the West Coast increased 10.9% from October 19, while capacity to the East Coast rose 11.4%.
“Offered capacity is increasing on all fronthauls out of the Far East to Europe and the U.S., with average spot rates unsurprisingly continuing to soften – with one exception,” said Peter Sand, Xeneta chief analyst.
Trans-Pacific rates remain sharply above year-ago
Despite the declines, trans-Pacific spot rates remained roughly four times their year-earlier levels. Far East–U.S. West Coast rates were up 304.3% from November 19, 2025, while East Coast rates were 297.8% higher.
The figures show that the latest easing has done little to erase the substantial year-over-year increase in shipping costs on either U.S. trade lane.
Trade lane | Spot rate, November 19 | Weekly change | Year-over-year change | Monthly offered capacity change*
Far East–U.S. West Coast | $8,203/FEU | -1.7% | 304.3% | 10.9%
Far East–U.S. East Coast | $10,901/FEU | -1.9% | 297.8% | 11.4%
Far East–North Europe | $3,438/FEU | -2.3% | 44.7% | 0.2%
Far East–Mediterranean | $4,989/FEU | 6.8% | 68.7% | 2.2%
North Europe–U.S. East Coast | $2,961/FEU | Effectively unchanged | 86.8% | 38.7%
(Source: Xeneta. Offered capacity changes compare four-week rolling averages with October 19, 2026.)
On the trans-Atlantic North Europe–U.S. East Coast route, rates were effectively unchanged for the week at $2,961 per FEU, despite offered capacity rising 38.7% from a month earlier. Rates on that trade remained 86.8% above year-earlier levels.
The U.S. market averted a possible strike at the Port of Los Angeles-Long Beach this past week as employers reached a tentative contract agreement with watchmen represented by the International Longshore and Warehouse Union .
Mediterranean bucks downward trend
The main exception to falling rates on Far East export trades was the Mediterranean, where average spot rates rose 6.8% to $4,989 per FEU despite a 2.2% monthly increase in offered capacity.
That pushed the Mediterranean premium over North Europe to $1,551 per FEU. Rates to North Europe fell 2.3% during the week to $3,438.
Sand said a slowdown in container shipping’s return to the Red Sea may help explain the divergence.
Container ship transits through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea increased from 305 in August to 463 in October. That recovery subsequently reversed, with the seven-day average falling 28% from a peak of 16.6 daily transits on October 25 to 11.9 on November 19.
“Something has happened to cool the return of container shipping services to the Red Sea in November,” Sand said. “Whatever the reason, disruption in the Red Sea is felt more acutely on trades between the Far East and the Mediterranean because they are the most operationally exposed to the region.”
Attacks on shipping continue to encompass a wide geographical range. Ukraine launched drone attacks on Russian ships in Libya, and vessels have been targeted off Bulgaria and Romania in the Black Sea, as well as in the Baltics.
Why It Matters: For U.S. importers, cargo owners and forwarders, expanding trans-Pacific capacity and declining weekly spot rates point to some easing in shipping costs, but rates remain roughly four times year-ago levels.

MCACN 2026: Chrysler 300 Display Brings Together All Letter Series Models (1955-1965)
19 photos
Photo: Jay Moser/YouTube
The 2026 Muscle Car and Corvette Nationals (MCACN) took place this weekend, bringing hundreds of classic muscle cars under the same roof. But this year's edition also included a very cool Chrysler 300 display. Reserved for "letter series" cars, it featured vehicles from each model year.
The "letter series" debuted in 1955 as the first Chrysler to sport the 300 emblem. It's called the "letter series" because each version had a different letter next to its 300 suffix. The series began with the C-300, but the cars built from 1956 to 1965 were named 300B to 300L. Chrysler skipped the letter I.
The original C-300 was in fact a homologation special. Essentially a full-size hardtop with a beefed-up engine, it was offered for public consumption so that Chrysler would be able to race it in NASCAR. The 1955 version featured a 331-cubic-inch (5.4-liter) FirePower V8 rated at 300 horsepower, hence the 300 name. Chrysler sold 1,725 units.
In 1956, Chrysler increased output to 340 horsepower but also offered a higher compression ratio variant of the engine good for 355 horsepower. The latter made the 300B the first American car to produce one horsepower per cubic inch. Design changes were minimal, and sales dropped to 1,102 examples.
Photo: Jay Moser/YouTube The 300C arrived in 1957 with a more flamboyant design. Additionally, the "letter series" gained a larger 392-cubic-inch (6.4-liter) Hemi good for 375 horsepower. Some 18 examples got a 390-horsepower version of the mill. The 300C was the first "letter series" model available as a convertible. Deliveries rose to 2,402 units.
Largely similar to the 300C, the 1958 300D was the last "letter series" to use the FirePower Hemi V8. It was now rated at 380 horsepower, with a fuel-injected version available (390 horsepower). The latter, however, was quickly discontinued due to reliability issues. The 300D moved only 809 examples.
The 300E arrived in 1959 with minor styling changes but with big news under the hood. The FirePower unit was dropped in favor of the 413-cubic-inch (6.8-liter) Golden Lion V8 . Rated at 380 horsepower, the 300E found 647 customers.
The Golden Lion remained in use in 1960, but output dropped slightly to 375 horsepower. However, Chrysler produced a 400-horsepower "short ram" version. The 300F had brand-new styling, but the large rear fins were still a thing. A four-speed manual was available for the first time. Sales recovered and reached 1,217 examples.
Photo: Jay Moser/YouTube The 1961 300G arrived with yet another redesign, which included slanted quad headlamps and smaller tailfins. Output remained unchanged at 375 horsepower, while the special-order four-speed manual was no longer available. The three-speed unit returned. Exactly 1,617 examples were delivered that year.
The 300H version of 1962 retained the previous year's front clip, but the rear fins were entirely gone. Still powered by the Golden Lion V8, the 300H came with 380 horsepower on tap. 1962 saw the introduction of the not-so-exclusive Chrysler 300 Sport . "Letter series" sales reached a new low, with only 570 units delivered.
For 1963, the 300J returned to quad horizontal headlamps while gaining a more angular trapezoidal grille. The Golden Lion was, again, Chrysler's choice for oomph, increasing output to 390 horsepower. The convertible version was no longer available for the first time since 1956. The four-speed manual became available. With only 400 units sold, the 300J is the rarest "letter series" car out there.
Chrysler made only minor adjustments to the design, but the 1964 300K arrived with a four-barrel version of the Golden Lion as standard. It was rated at 360 horsepower. The cross-ram version was now an option. The convertible returned, and Chrysler made the "letter series" a bit cheaper by removing some luxury items. Sales reached an all-time high at 3,647 examples.
Photo: Jay Moser/YouTube The final iteration of the "letter series," the 1965 300L , arrived with a brand-new styling with crisp lines and slab sides. The cross-ram unit was removed from the options list, with the four-barrel 413 Golden Lion remaining the sole powerplant. Output was 360 horsepower, as in the previous year. The 300L sold 2,845 units. Although Chrysler showed a clay model of the 1966 300M in late 1963, the car never went into production.
The MCACN display is obviously packed with nicely restored models, but it also includes a few cars we may never see somewhere else. The list includes the 1958 300D pilot car (the first ever built, also fitted with the fuel-injected engine) and the supercharged 1960 300F that reached nearly 180 mph (290 kph) at Daytona. An unrestored 1961 300G was also on display.
Hit the play button below to check them all out. And when you do, tell me which one you liked the most in the comments section below. I'm a big fan of the first-year C-300, but I also love the 1957 300C and 1961 300G. The finless 1962 300H also looks cool in the convertible layout.

By Charlotte Goldstone
23 November 2026
Shipping faces additional regulatory burdens, higher freight costs, and prolonged uncertainty if governments fail to agree meaningful economic measures this month, warned maritime emissions specialists.
Ahead of the International Maritime Organization (IMO) Marine Environment Protection Committee meeting (MEPC 85), in London from 30 November to 4 December, OceanScore MD Albrecht Grell warned that negotiations focusing on technical measures could undermine investment in cleaner fuels and vessels.
“If only technical measures can be agreed, more measuring, tracking, and reporting work will be forced upon shipping without any real progress towards net-zero shipping,” he told The Loadstar .
“My concern is that the discussion increasingly centres around technical measures. Standalone, these are not helpful – think of CII,” he added, referring to the IMO’s Carbon Intensity Indicator.
Mr Grell argued that economic measures were essential to stimulating investment in alternative-fuel production, fleet renewal, and fuel-ready vessels. He pointed to the impact of the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) and FuelEU Maritime, which he estimated affected only around 30% of the global fleet.
“A meaningful IMO Net-Zero Framework (NZF) could help to close that gap,” he said.
However, failure to agree economic measures could delay an effective IMO NFZ for a prolonged period, potentially encouraging more countries to introduce their own emissions regulations, he added.
His comments follow a joint appeal from nine shipping associations, including BIMCO, the International Chamber of Shipping (ICS) and World Shipping Council (WSC), urging governments to establish a global greenhouse gas framework providing investment certainty and preventing overlapping regional requirements.
Friederike Hesse, co-founder and MD of maritime emissions management specialist zero44, told The Loadstar that although IMO member states had become “more constructive”, a final agreement was more likely in 2027 than at December’s meeting.
She highlighted that governments had previously converged on several principles, including prioritising emissions reductions, allowing ships to trade compliance surpluses and incentivising zero-emission fuels. However, disagreements remained over the ambition and duration of emissions targets and how revenues would be used.
Ms Hesse warned that continued uncertainty would carry direct commercial consequences, adding: “Uncertainty itself is a cost. Companies price-in risk premiums, put their eggs in multiple baskets instead of focusing investments, add contractual buffers, and spend more on legal and administrative work – and that ends up in freight rates.”
She also warned that delaying emissions reductions would require steeper cuts later, potentially leaving fuel production and fleet renewal struggling to keep pace.
“Postponing cuts doesn’t make them disappear,” she urged, warning that the resulting transition could become more expensive and risk disruption to global trade.
For shipowners and fuel suppliers making investments over 20 to 30 years, regulatory uncertainty could discourage fuel offtake agreements and slow alternative-fuel production.
Mr Grell argued that decarbonisation costs would ultimately fall on cargo owners, although operators’ ability to adapt would determine the impact on profitability.
“Shipping is highly competitive – any cost will eventually be passed on to the cargo owners,” he said. “The profit pool will not change but be redistributed within the industry.”
Both experts warned against proliferating regional schemes without effective global regulation. Ms Hesse said this could concentrate alternative-fuel infrastructure around regulated markets, rather than global trade routes, while exposing operators to overlapping compliance obligations.
Mr Grell agreed: “Nobody benefits from overlapping reporting regimes, admin layers and compliance efforts.”
According to Ms Hesse, regional measures such as the EU ETS should complement an eventual IMO framework, potentially recognising payments already made under global rules.
“Whether regional schemes disappear entirely matters less than making sure no tonne of CO₂ is charged twice,” she said.

All-Black Aptera Is the World’s First Production Solar Electric Vehicle, Heading to Indonesia
15 photos
Photo: Aptera
It's been a long time coming, but here we finally are, ready to tell the world that its first-ever production vehicle powered by the Sun is here. It's called the Aptera, after the name of the company making it, comes in matte black, and is bound not for the U.S., where it is built, but for Indonesia.
Aptera Motors announced at the end of last week that the first vehicle meant for a customer rolled off the lines at its facility in Carlsbad, California. The buyer, we're told, is Indonesian businessman Martin Hartono, who also happens to be an investor who has backed Aptera's plans for such a contraption.
You see, as most other startups out there, Aptera's business model relied a lot on investors. In the company speak, they are called Accelerators, and Hartono is number 1, based on the amount of money invested – hence the honor of him receiving the first vehicle.
The subsequent vehicles are reserved for the other Accelerators, but the company does not specify who or how many of them are out there. What's clear, though, is that their number is far lower than the 50,000 people the company claims have already reserved their own solar-powered cars.
The three-wheeled vehicle is officially classified as an autocycle, and it was presented in its current form at the 2025 Consumer Electronics Show (CES) in Las Vegas. It is powered by an electric powertrain comprising a 40-kWh liquid-cooled battery and an electric motor. Nothing spectacular here, but the way the battery is charged kind of is.
Ok, one can charge the thing the old-fashioned way, by plugging it into a charging station, as it comes equipped with a North American Charging System (NACS) connector, but they can also use the solar panels installed on the roof for that.
There are 700 watts-worth of solar cells up there, and they can send more than four kWh of solar energy into the battery under ideal conditions. That's enough to allow the vehicle to travel for as many as 40 miles (64 km) on free, solar power alone. The total distance the battery is good for is rated at 400 miles (644 km).
The electric motor that gets its juice from the battery allows for an acceleration time of six seconds from zero to 60 mph, while the top speed, with the maximum of two people on board, stands at 100 mph (161 kph).
The carbon fiber body of the Aptera wraps around a cabin fitted with only a steering yoke, a center display, and a couple of additional displays tied into external cameras, which act as side rearview mirrors.
There are some safety features included in the design, including a safety cell, an energy-absorbing front nose cone, and a subframe designed to crumple on impact, but no airbags, ABS, or any driver assistance feature. All of that for a starting price of around $40,000.

In updated Phase 1 data, Erasca’s ERAS-0015 showed a robust response rate in pancreatic cancer subgroups where Revolution Medicines’ recently-approved Rasonque was weaker, leading Jefferies to write that the investigational molecular glue could have an advantage over the approved therapy.
Erasca reported more early data Friday for its molecular glue candidate ERAS-0015 left some analysts bullish as the biotech looks to go up against Revolution Medicines in the pancreatic cancer space.
ERAS‑0015, a pan-RAS molecular glue, “showed the profile needed to challenge [RevMed’s] daraxonrasib,” Jefferies analysts wrote in a Friday note to investors. Daraxonrasib was approved as Rasonque in August after doubling survival in a Phase 3 study of pancreatic cancer.
In the Phase 1 AURORAS-1 trial, ERAS-0015 led to a 44% confirmed overall response rate (ORR)—one of the trial’s secondary endpoints—in 25 patients with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) with KRAS G12X mutations who had already tried at least one other treatment, according to the biotech . Digging deeper into the data, 69% of 13 patients with KRAS G12D or G12V mutations responded to once-daily treatment with 32 mg of ERAS-0015. Erasca said these subgroups represent nearly 70% of patients with PDAC in the general population.
The Phase 1 trial is also studying ERAS-0015 in KRAS G12X-mutated non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), where the same treatment regimen scored a 60% confirmed ORR in five patients.
As for safety, which was measured by several of AURORAS-1’s primary endpoints, the frequency and severity of treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs) remained consistent with Erasca’s previous interim data disclosures in April and July. Treatment-related adverse events (TRAE) were mostly low-grade, with no dose-limiting toxicities and a low rate of dose interruptions, reductions and discontinuations due to TRAEs, Erasca said.
Rasonque, approved for second-line pancreatic cancer, elicited a 33% ORR across all KRAS mutations in the Phase 3 RASolute 302 trial. However, the drug’s performance in patients with G12D mutations, which represented 43% of the trial’s population, led to an ORR of just 24%, according to FDA review documents released in October. A smaller cohort with G12R mutations saw just a 7% ORR.

“We think ’0015 could be advantageous over daraxonrasib in PDAC, given its stronger G12D/V activity and the unusually high proportion of less-sensitive G12R pts in the ph. 1 dataset,” Jefferies said.
Analysts at Leerink Partners were more cautious regarding Erasca’s updated data.
“Erasca’s maiden medical meeting debut for ERAS-0015 was supportive of the drug’s differentiation potential, but the data at the most meaningful monotherapy dose (32mg) is still very early and in a small sample,” they wrote on Friday.
The response rates for ERAS-0015 were “in line with or above expectations set by management - and are numerically favorable, particularly given the difficult patient mix,” Leerink added. However, the analysts continued, the 32-mg dose “needs more sample and follow up to give the cross trial comp more credibility.”
That said, the firm noted that “deal allure” is still on the table for Erasca. “We maintain that ERAS could give Pharma deal-makers access to a coveted clinical-stage pan-RAS agent,” the analysts wrote.
One company that appears to be interested in the therapy’s potential is Bristol Myers Squibb, which last week entered into a clinical trial collaboration and supply agreement with Erasca to study ERAS-0015 with its investigational PRMT5 inhibitor navlimetostat.
Erasca is accelerating its plans to launch a Phase 3 trial in first-line pancreatic cancer to the first half of 2027. RevMed is similarly pursuing a first-line indication for Rasonque, last week sharing early-stage data that exceeded analyst expectations in this setting.
Erasca is also planning a Phase 3 trial in patients with first-line RAS-mutant NSCLC to begin in the second half of next year or the first half of 2028. RevMed, meanwhile, is actively recruiting for a Phase 3 study of daraxonrasib in second-line or later NSCLC.
Erasca and RevMed are not shaping up to be friendly competitors in the pancreatic cancer space. In April, RevMed claimed that ERAS-0015 was “substantially equivalent” to certain formulations used in daraxonrasib. “Moving ERAS-0015 forward, according to RevMed, would infringe on patent protections, according to a letter Erasca received from that company’s legal counsel,” per an SEC filing .

Posted By: FREDERIC TOMESCO November 23, 2026
First Mining Gold (TSX: FF; US-OTC: FFMGF) has received Ontario’s environmental-assessment approval for the Springpole project in northwestern Ontario as it looks to finance a proposed $1.1 billion (C$1.6 billion) open-pit operation. The stock soared.
Ontario Environment Minister Todd McCarthy approved the assessment for the project 400 km northeast of Thunder Bay, First Mining announced Monday . Ottawa had approved the project on June 30. The company is targeting completion of a feasibility study and project financing in 2027, ahead of a construction decision in 2028. Further project permits and authorizations are still required.
“While provincial approval was anticipated, its receipt is a major de-risking milestone and materially improves visibility toward feasibility, financing and construction and is consistent with our development assumptions,” National Bank Financial mining analyst Alex Terentiew said in a note.
When considering formalized agreements in place with local First Nations communities, “Springpole has now secured the principal environmental and social approvals required to advance toward a development decision,” Terentiew added. “Secondary permits, financing and board approval remain outstanding, but the key permitting risk underpinning our thesis has now been removed.” First Mining shares jumped 7.5% to 57¢ Monday morning in Toronto, valuing the company at about C$850 million ($590 million). They’ve traded between 30.5¢ and 98¢ over the past year.
Execution focus
Investor focus will now shift to execution instead of environmental assessment, Terentiew said.
Part of the deposit lies beneath Springpole Lake. First Mining plans to build two dykes and drain part of the lake to reach the ore. Under federal conditions, it must establish at least one Indigenous environmental committee before construction. The committees will help monitor water quality and measures to protect caribou.
“This land will always be home to our people long after the Springpole Project has ended,” Lac Seul First Nation Chief Clifford Bull said in August, when his nation and Cat Lake First Nation signed a benefits agreement with the company.
First Mining held C$81 million in cash and marketable securities at Sept. 30 after raising gross proceeds of C$57.5 million in a September share sale. The company plans an 18-km all-weather access road, a construction camp and a power connection. It already has permits for a winter road to resupply its existing camp.
Springpole could produce 330,000 payable oz. gold a year in its first five years and average 281,000 oz. over a 9.4-year mine life, First Mining estimated in a 2025 prefeasibility study . At a gold price of $3,100 per oz., the project had an after-tax net present value of $2.1 billion at a 5% discount rate and a 41% internal rate of return. Initial capital costs were estimated at $1.1 billion.
Cat Lake and Lac Seul conducted their own impact assessment before reaching an August agreement to share in the project’s financial benefits. First Mining also signed a separate agreement with Slate Falls Nation that month.

Ford Ranger Super Duty Hy-Rail Conversion Reports for Railway Work
15 photos
Photo: Ford
The Ranger Super Duty has already undertaken plenty of jobs that would overwhelm a regular mid-size pickup. Its latest conversion, however, ups the ante to railway work. Together with Ford Pro's Convertor division, Australian specialist Aries Rail has developed a hy-rail system that lets the diesel-powered truck drive along railway tracks.
Ford engineers helped Aries integrate the hardware into the chassis, and the Dearborn-based automaker further made a bunch of modifications to the SYNC infotainment system for this application. Aries Rail spent four decades doing such conversions with a bunch of different vehicles, but the Ranger Super Duty program is on another level altogether.
Railway operators use road-rail vehicles to inspect tracks, clear obstacles, and send maintenance crews to sections where ordinary automobiles cannot reach. Aries Rail's solution starts with a quartet of flanged steel guide wheels that are raised or lowered hydraulically.
Joining the 70-series Toyota Land Cruiser hy-rail conversion, the Ranger Super Duty program gives Aries Rail another platform to work with. The heavy-duty axles, thicker driveshafts, upgraded suspension, and reinforced chassis all recommended the Ranger Super Duty for this job, and Aries Rail wanted to exploit all of those attributes without compromising the underlying vehicle's usability.
The collab started in 2025, with Ford Pro Converter providing the engineering support. Under this program, approved converters receive the mounting manual that explains how to work with the Ranger Super Duty's structure and mounting points. Aries Rail also used computer-aided design data to develop a unique installation rather than adapt an existing rail system for the Ranger Super Duty.
Photo: Ford Ford helped Aries optimize the mounting and installation, and Ford's involvement in the project avoided compromising the vehicle's warranty. The cabin required just as much attention, and this brings us to a company dubbed Opses.
The technology partner came up with an integrated solution for the Ranger Super Duty hy-rail conversion, routing the controls for the hydraulic rail guidance system through the SYNC infotainment display instead of adding another display or switch panel. Aries had never integrated the rail guidance controls this way before.
A standardized conversion process allows Aries to build the same configuration over and over again at its facilities around Australia, which makes the conversion particularly relevant to commercial customers. A fleet operator needs consistency across the board, and having an identical conversion process makes everything easier on both sides.
Ariel Rail sees opportunities beyond the Australian market, with chief executive officer Nathan Bender claiming that said conversion could eventually become a global product. Neither Aries nor Ford announced international sales plans or specific export markets. For the time being, the demo vehicle will have to suffice at the AusRAIL 2026 in Brisbane, which runs through November 25, 2026.
The steel wheels are there only for guidance, which means the rubber wheels and V6 diesel engine do the heavy lifting on railroad tracks. Similar to the standard Ranger Super Duty, the 3.0-liter unit is connected to a 10-speed auto box and produces 154 kW (207 hp) at full chatter. Its peak torque is estimated at 600 Newton-meters, a figure that can be read as 443 pound-feet in the US market where Ford doesn't sell this fellow.

Invivyd plans on ushering in a “new era for immunization” with its COVID-19 prevention antibody that is designed using the same antibody backbone as the biotech’s emergency-authorized Pemgarda.
Invivyd’s next-gen monoclonal antibody is estimated to protect against 70-90% of symptomatic COVID-19 infections in a Phase 3 interim analysis, teeing up accelerated approval submission plans for the first quarter of 2027.
The readout garnered the support of Robert Redfield, who led the CDC from 2018 to 2021. The American virologist does not have any public ties to the biotech.
“Invivyd is making possible what has been elusive for years: giving people true protection from symptomatic COVID infection without experiencing inflammation and the safety and tolerability challenges of COVID-19 vaccines,” Redfield said in Invivyd’s Monday release .
The fresh data centers on Declaration , a late-stage trial for monoclonal antibody VYD2311, also known as ibramvibart. The drug was delivered via intramuscular (IM) injection either once or three times 30 days apart in people at least 12 years old, with the study covering the 90-day response after the first shot. The study enrolled 1,770 people, randomizing participants to receive either placebo or the investigational antibody, which is designed to glom onto the virus that causes COVID-19 and stop it from entering cells.
In the interim analysis, VYD2311 demonstrated durable antiviral activity predictive of clinical protection levels of 70-90% at 90 days for both dosing groups as compared to placebo—the trial’s primary endpoint.
This compares to data Invivyd pulled for traditional COVID-19 vaccines, estimating a 30-35% reduction in medically attended COVID-19 for 90 days. Efficacy figures range widely across medical literature, with a New England Journal of Medicine analysis of numerous studies finding mRNA vaccines against the circulating COVID-19 variant had a pooled effectiveness against hospitalization of 46%.

Invivyd is keeping the clinical COVID-19 events fully blinded to support a potential traditional approval application.
For analysts with H.C. Wainwright, the readout “support VYD2311’s potential as a broadly used IM prophylactic,” with the firm reiterating a “buy” rating for the company’s stock. In particular, the analysts highlighted the drug’s single-dose profile as commercially important, while noting that the interim analysis remains a projection.
“Today marks the dawn of a new era in our 300-year history of human immunization,” Invivyd CEO Marc Elia said in a prepared statement. “People have long sought new options for protection against COVID infection, and we intend to make VYD2311 available soon.”
Invivyd will combine the Declaration data with the late-stage Liberty findings , which read out in September and found VYD2311 was superior in safety and tolerability compared to an mRNA-based COVID-19 vaccine, according to the Connecticut biotech.
The company has been in talks with both HHS and the FDA regarding potential regulatory pathways and expects a biologics licensing application (BLA) review to be conducted by or with input from the FDA’s Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research (CBER).
VYD2311 was created using Invivyd’s platform that is designed to neutralize contemporary virus lineages. The candidate has the same antibody backbone as Pemgarda—or pemivibart—a monoclonal antibody that secured FDA emergency use authorization in 2024 for the pre-exposure prophylaxis of symptomatic COVID-19 in certain immunocompromised patients.
The biotech—which rebranded from Adagio Therapeutics in 2022—is also developing adintrevimab, another monoclonal antibody that provided prophylactic efficacy against COVID-19 in a Phase 2/3 trial amid the omicron variant wave.
“Invivyd’s work with monoclonal antibodies, starting with adintrevimab, and then pemivibart, and now including VYD2311, has the potential to quickly become standard of care and stop COVID in its tracks,” former CDC director Redfield added in the release.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang delivers remarks as President Donald Trump looks on during an “Investing in America” event on April 30, 2025, at the White House. Credit: Official White House Photo by Joyce N. Boghosian.
Posted By: Northern Miner Staff November 23, 2026
Uranium stocks rallied Monday after Nvidia (Nasdaq: NVDA) brought back co-founder Jensen Huang as CEO. Cameco (TSX: CCO; NYSE: CCJ) gained 7.4% in New York, recovering some of the ground uranium miners lost when Huang stepped down this month.
Cameco traded at $62.30 (C$89.24) around 9:42 a.m. Toronto time, while Energy Fuels (TSX: EFR; NYSE-A: UUUU) climbed 11% to $5.51. The Sprott Uranium Miners ETF (NYSE Arca: URNM) rose 6.3% to $35.74 as Nvidia jumped 26% to $158.11.
“Uranium stocks used to trade on uranium. Now they trade with AI,” David Talbot, a mining analyst and head of equity research at Red Cloud Securities, wrote Monday.
Tech, shares link
Technology companies’ deals to buy nuclear power for their data centres helped drive uranium shares higher last year, Talbot said. The same link punished miners when artificial intelligence stocks fell. From Jan. 28 through Nov. 19, the Sprott fund lost 57% even as uranium market consultant UxC’s long-term price for uranium oxide (U 3 O 8 ) rose 10% to $97 per pound.
Nvidia’s board voted unanimously Sunday to reinstate Huang , whose departure the chipmaker announced Nov. 12. After hearing from senior U.S. officials, directors concluded his return posed no national security risk. Independent directors are still investigating reports that a foreign intelligence operation targeted him, Nvidia said Monday .
The sell-off around Huang’s departure fit a pattern Talbot traced back to July 2025. On the 58 trading days when a fund tracking AI stocks fell more than 1.5%, Sprott’s miners fund fell 88% of the time, he found.
Nuclear demand rising
Demand for reactor fuel has kept growing. Nearly 90 gigawatts of nuclear capacity was under construction worldwide by midyear, the most in more than 35 years, the International Energy Agency said in its Nov. 19 outlook . Utilities still need to contract for about 768 million lb. of U 3 O 8 through 2035, Talbot said, citing UxC.
“Nothing in this morning’s news changes reactor demand or uranium supply, so it does not change the fundamental case for the uranium stocks,” Talbot wrote after Nvidia announced Huang’s return.

EREVs May Dodge EU Hybrid Caps but Still Face BEV Tariffs
19 photos
Photo: Leapmotor
The European Union's planned restrictions on hybrid vehicle imports may create an opening for Chinese automakers in particular. Electric vehicles equipped with range-extended powertrains may avoid the proposed limits, even as plug-in hybrids and conventional hybrids face tighter access into the EU. There is, however, a catch that has to be highlighted.
According to Nikkei, extended-range electric vehicles could remain subject to the European bloc's existing anti-subsidy duties on Chinese battery-electric vehicles. In other words, Chinese manufacturers would be left with a choice between potentially higher import costs and restricted sales.
Before going any further, a plug-in hybrid is a different animal from an extended-range electric vehicle because PHEVs can provide mechanical propulsion. EREVs, meanwhile, use their internal combustion engines to supply electricity to the electric drive system and the traction battery, with propulsion handled exclusively by the electric motor(s) even with a low state of charge.
A seemingly narrow distinction, for sure. The European Commission's existing customs treatment places EREVs in the BEV category instead of grouping them with hybrids. Naturally, this means that extended-range electric vehicles fall outside the classifications covered by the proposed hybrid import restrictions.
Said classification traces its roots back to Regulation 2024/2754, which classified these vehicles under customs code 8703 80 10 as battery-electric vehicles. The reasoning? An engine that only generates electricity doesn't make the vehicle a conventional hybrid in the relevant customs classification.
Photo: Leapmotor Hybrids and plug-in hybrids are listed under customs codes 8703 40 10, 8703 50 00, 8703 60 10, and 8703 70 00, depending on configuration. Given the aforementioned, EREVs may escape the proposed annual import ceiling for hybrids without escaping the current BEV penalties.
Chinese battery-electric vehicles face European countervailing duties of up to 35.3 percent, depending on the automaker, plus the bloc's 10 percent import duty. These duties would continue to apply to qualifying EREVs imported from the People's Republic of China, which is the largest market for new passenger vehicles in terms of domestic sales. Around 24 million were sold there in 2025 alone.
Nikkei underlines that pricing and profitability would still be a problem with Chinese manufacturers, which may pass part of the costs to customers. In this case, EREVs would become less competitive in the European market. On the other hand, Chinese automakers could very well agree to less money on each imported EREV as long as they create a niche for themselves in the European space.
Leapmotor, which produces the Euro-market B10 crossover at the Stellantis Zaragoza plant in Spain, offers an EREV option. Marketed as the REEV Hybrid in the Spanish market, said model uses a rear-mounted electric motor that delivers 160 kW (215 hp) and 240 Nm (177 lb-ft) of twist. Up front, a 1.5-liter naturally aspirated I4 powers the onboard generator, rated at 50 kW (67 hp) by its maker.
A lithium-iron-phosphate battery with 18.8 kWh also needs mentioning, with Leapmotor Espana promising up to 86 kilometers (53 miles) of electric driving range. In the WLTP cycle, total combined range is estimated at 900 kilometers (559 miles) with a full charge and a full tank of dinosaur juice.

The fresh food trade is growing and rearranging itself at the same time. GLP-1 drugs are changing what people eat, tariffs are redrawing where product comes from, new companies keep arriving in fresh fruit, and a steady run of M&A keeps changing who trades with whom. Every one of those shifts puts a grower, a wholesaler or a carrier in front of a counterparty they have never dealt with before.
Brad Guinane, Blue Book’s president of supply chain solutions, made the case at F3, in a conversation with Will Hopping, chief product and technology officer at Sonar, that the company’s 125-year record of how businesses actually behave is what lets those trades happen at all. A fake identity can be built in minutes. A payment history takes decades, and that gap cuts both ways: it is how you catch an impersonator, and it is how a company nobody has traded with yet proves it is worth trading with. Blue Book helps farmers, growers, wholesalers, retailers and logistics companies find and vet one another, and it steps in when claims and collections issues arise.
Guinane said AI has made it far easier to pose as one of those trusted partners.
“What you can do with AI and two minutes to create a website that’s a lookalike and change a letter on an email and go call a farmer or a wholesaler and say you are someone who you are not, that can now happen way easier than it ever could before,” he said.
Impersonation is the most common scheme
Impersonation attempts are the threat Blue Book sees most often, Guinane said. Many companies in the trade have little digital footprint, and in peak season a perishable load has to leave the warehouse fast.
“It’s very easy to say, I’ll change a letter or I’ll give you a call and say, I am this company and I need to move 20 crates of strawberries and go do it for me. And then I’d go do something else with it,” he said.
Guinane said several data points show fraud rising, while noting it is unclear how much went recorded in the past.
Payment history works as an identity check
That record is the reason both halves work. Blue Book sees about $70 billion a year in accounts receivable data, almost all of it from its roughly 5,000 produce and logistics customers plus some factoring companies, Guinane said. The data shows who owes what and whether a company pays in 30 days or 45, and Blue Book’s internal ratings team uses it to build each company’s rating.
Blue Book also sends about 60,000 surveys a day and gets one back every 30 seconds, he said. Trading partners use them to report how a company pays and any claims they have had with it.
A lookalike website has none of that behind it.
“It becomes very difficult to fake a ten, fifteen, twenty, thirty, forty year history,” he said.
Some food companies require whoever transports their goods to hold a Blue Book number, a rating, and a history, Guinane said. Since joining, he has been struck by “the number of customers that we actually get that come from our existing customer base saying, you have to be a part of this in order for me to work with you.”
When a trade does go wrong
The record also does work after a deal closes. Blue Book runs claims and collections for members, which is the part of the business that returns money rather than preventing its loss, and the same payment history that identifies a counterparty up front is what gets a stalled invoice moving.
A certificate for handling perishables
A Blue Book rating covers payment behavior and claims. Customers also asked for a check on how their partners handle perishables, Guinane said: “How can we ensure that partners that we’re working with understand how to handle fresh products, perishables?”
Blue Book answered with a certification it recently released, built with its produce, floral, and nursery customers. Guinane said companies are using it to set themselves apart, and Blue Book plans to keep adding checks like it.
“How do we help our customers differentiate themselves?” Guinane said. Companies are using the credential to win work rather than simply to qualify for it, and Blue Book plans to keep adding checks like it.
Next come integrations and new categories
The company’s data has moved from a printed book to a software platform updated daily and weekly. Guinane said the next step is feeding that data into MCP and updating Blue Book’s APIs so customers can integrate it at the CRM and ERP level.
Beyond produce, Blue Book already rates floral and nursery companies, and Guinane said it plans to cover more of the grocery store.
“Think about walking into a grocery store and seeing all of the food that is in the refrigerated section from meats to frozen,” he said. “Blue Book will be there, and we’ll be providing data and insights to help people transact safely.”
To learn more visit Blue Book Services.

U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping shake hands as they depart following a bilateral meeting at Gimhae Air Base on October 30, 2025 in Busan, South Korea. (Photo by Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
When President Donald Trump descended the stairs from Air Force One in Shenzhen, China, he was greeted with a hug from China’s Xi Jinping. And why not? It’s easy to imagine Xi is in a pretty good mood these days, thanks to the early conclusions Chinese planners are likely drawing from the 2026 American midterm elections.
Determining American political vulnerabilities is an essential part of preparing the political terrain for exploitation in any future crisis. For Xi, understanding what American voters will and won’t tolerate will provide direct insights into how China should act during any potential conflicts in the near and long term. And when it comes to takeaways from the election, there are two that Beijing is likely to focus on: the American public’s appetite for conflict, and the American public’s apprehension around artificial intelligence.
Both could have major impacts on Chinese planners when thinking about the short term, such as a potential Taiwan conflict, and the long-term with its great power competition with Washington.
Past Chinese analyses have highlighted the apparent reluctance of the American electorate to sustain wars in the face of casualties. Chinese military analysts have pointed to the American withdrawal from Somalia in 1993 after the “Blackhawk Down” fiasco. They have also suggested that the reason the US bombed Serbia while refraining from committing ground forces was a similar fear of suffering casualties. No doubt April’s massive US effort in Iran to rescue a downed F-15E crew reinforces this view. The implication is that the prospect of suffering significant casualties is likely to deter, or at least slow down, American leaders and make them reconsider their commitments.
But interestingly, the current conflict with Iran has not seen significant American casualties. The US has suffered several dozen killed and several hundred wounded, for which it has inflicted massive losses on the Iranian armed forces and decapitated much of the Iranian leadership. Nonetheless, as even Vice President JD Vance observed, the war with Iran was a huge factor in the Republican loss of the House and Senate.
In this election year, the impact was not from human casualties, but economic losses. The closure of the Straits of Hormuz, as much because of the maritime insurance industry’s fears of losses as actual damage to shipping inflicted by Tehran, led to rising oil prices, which in turn affected pricing of all other goods and services. And the costs persist, as the conflict continues to extract a toll on domestic economics.
It is therefore likely that a key takeaway that Beijing will factor into its preparations for any conflict over Taiwan is ensuring that the war will impact the American voters . Given the heavy Chinese presence in various supply chains, especially of consumer goods, it is likely that the Chinese will restrict the flow of goods to Walmart and Amazon, as well as rare earth minerals, while at the same time boycotting American goods in China. The goal would be to cause disruptions in the American economy that would directly affect the voting public.
But as students of history, the Chinese also likely expected the Republicans to lose at least one of the houses of Congress, as is typical of mid-term elections. They likely did not anticipate the electorate’s mass disdain for data centers and, by association, artificial intelligence. In 41 ballot initiatives in 10 states, all but one resulted in measures to limit future data center development. Nationwide, data centers were not only a major part of debates, but the American electorate has broadly rejected their unfettered expansion.
For Beijing, this is an enormously important development.
From the Chinese Communist Party’s (CCP) perspective, with the massive growth and expansion of information and communications technologies (ICT), humanity transitioned from the Industrial Age to the Information Age in the 1990s. The currency of power shifted to the ability to generate, move, analyze and exploit information more rapidly and more accurately than your competitor or adversary. The shift to the Information Age altered the underpinnings of everything from military security to economic development to genetic engineering and medical research. Developments such as cell phones, the internet and the proliferation of computers and tablets led to a massive expansion of person-to-person and organization-to-organization information sharing. The Chinese termed this “informationization” (alternately translated as “informatization” and “informationalization”).
The transition is ongoing, with continuing advances in ICT. The result has been “intelligence-ization” (alternately translated as “intelligentization”). Where previous information sharing and exploitation continued to have a heavy human component, this is now evolving to machine-to-machine information movement, without human intervention. This is the key to such developments as the Internet of Things, networks of self-driving cars, “smart cities,” and drone swarms. Whether it is future cities or future battlefields, the ability of machines to interact with other machines, at the speed of algorithmic “thought,” will be a key determinant of winners — and losers.
In a 2025 session with the CCP’s top leadership, Xi emphasized that Chinese AI development must not only involve developing technical AI capabilities, but its incorporation into a broad range of economic activities. That is, AI is not just about advancing R&D, but applying it to existing industries and services — including the military.
In this environment, the gap between Chinese and American views of AI is striking. According to the Stanford AI index, over 80 percent of Chinese are excited by the prospects of artificial intelligence, over double that of American respondents. As important, only one-third of those Americans surveyed said they would trust AI, against 72 percent of Chinese. It seems clear that Americans view AI with deep skepticism if not outright animosity, a view reflected in the mid-term election results.
Much as the Soviets tried to exploit the West’s anti-nuclear movements, it is likely the Chinese are similarly trying to capitalize on American and other Western anti-data center and anti-AI feelings. Regardless, there is clearly an anti-AI wave in the American public, which Beijing will no doubt be thrilled by.
In the competition between the US and PRC, the mid-terms suggest that Americans are not prepared to engage in the all-out competition the Chinese expect and are preparing for.
Dean Cheng is a non-resident fellow with the Potomac Institute for Policy Studies and with the George Washington University’s Space Policy Institute. When not translating Chinese articles, he can often be found feeding quarters into pinball machines.

He also confirmed that cars won’t get the next-gen AI5 chip, and that the mid-cycle AI4.5 upgrade just had its RAM cut from 32GB to 24GB.
Musk explains where AI4’s compute goes
The most visible part of FSD v15 is Tesla Reality View, a live, video-game-like rendering of the car’s surroundings with chevrons floating in the sky for upcoming turns. Musk called it “real-time AI video generation (no gaming engine!) using just half of one AI4 TRIP accelerator.”
The fan accounts ran with that as a flex. But Musk’s follow-up posts tell a different story.

He explained that after Tesla moved a decoder into SRAM, “we only have half a TRIP out of three on SoC B, for this reality visualizer, so spent the compute as best we could.” In other words, half a TRIP is what was left over. He added that TRIP, Tesla’s neural accelerator, “basically only handles 8-bit int and has to run softmax in emulation mode in 28 steps.”
In another post , Musk described Reality View as a roughly 1-billion-parameter diffusion model running off the same vision encoder features “that are plugged into the 3B encoder model that produces the driving actions.” He admitted the visualization’s latency is “a bit high due to compute constraints.”
That 3B figure is worth noting. Tesla talked up a 10x jump in FSD model size for over a year, first for v14 and then for v15. Musk didn’t say whether 3B covers the entire driving stack, but it’s nowhere near 10x.
And Tesla’s own engineers aren’t describing a chip with lots of headroom. Dilreet Raju, who works on Tesla’s AI silicon, wrote that the hardest work of his life was co-designing the v15 vision encoder “to squeeze out the last few percents of MFU from AI4.” MFU is model FLOPs utilization, a measure of how much of the chip’s theoretical compute the model actually uses. Musk replied with a target emoji.
The redundancy problem
When Tesla unveiled its FSD computer in 2019, the selling point was redundancy: two independent chips on one board, each with its own power and memory, so one could take over if the other failed. As we noted when Tesla started shipping the AI4.5 computer in Model Y in January, Tesla’s FSD computers have historically used two identical chips for exactly that reason.
That’s what an unsupervised, Level 4 system needs. With nobody in the driver’s seat, a hardware fault can’t simply hand control back to a human. The car needs enough healthy compute left to keep seeing the road and pull over safely.
But Musk’s own description shows SoC B running the decoder and the Reality View model, not sitting idle as a mirror of SoC A. Tesla hackers, including greentheonly, have reported for years that Tesla started splitting its FSD workload across both chips back in the HW3 days.
Tesla has never explained how much of AI4 it reserves for failover, or whether a single SoC can run enough of the stack to bring a car to a safe stop on its own. The more of the board v15 needs, the harder that question gets.
Waymo has answered it publicly. The company says both of its onboard computing systems run full workloads in parallel and that a secondary computer can bring the vehicle to a safe stop if the primary fails, backed by redundant braking, steering and power. Its new custom chip is rated at more than 1,000 TOPS. By our own comparison of AI4 and Nvidia’s Drive Thor , AI4 is estimated at roughly 100 to 150 TOPS across both chips.
FSD v15 is still mostly in the hands of early testers
Tesla started rolling out FSD v15 on Saturday, claiming “25x better handling of safety critical cases” without any baseline. So far, the people posting videos are mostly the usual crowd of Tesla-focused accounts that get early builds. Just hours before the rollout started, Musk wrote that v15 “goes to wide release next month.”
The early clips are almost all about Reality View, the new parking spot selection, and the floating arrows. Those are UI features. They say very little about how many miles v15 can drive between critical interventions, which is the only number that matters for unsupervised driving.
AI4.5: more RAM, not much more speed
That brings us to AI4.5. On Tesla’s Q1 2026 earnings call, Musk announced an “AI4 Plus” with RAM doubled from 16GB to 32GB per chip, which raised the question of whether HW4 would follow HW3 .
This weekend, Musk said “AI4.5 is a relatively small performance improvement that is mostly due to needing to upgrade RAM to LPDDR5X.” Hours later, he added : “RAM is super expensive, so we reduced AI4.5 from 32GB to 24GB. That will be fine. It’s hard to use 32GB anyway, given memory bandwidth constraints.”
He also said that AI4 “costs twice as much now due to memory and storage price hikes.”
So the mid-cycle refresh exists mainly because Tesla needs a newer memory type it can actually buy, not to unlock bigger models. If memory bandwidth is the bottleneck, as Musk keeps repeating, adding capacity doesn’t change much.
AI5 and AI6 go to Optimus
Asked by an owner on Sunday whether to wait for AI5 before upgrading from HW3, Musk answered : “It’s going to Optimus. Cars will remain at AI4. That’s enough to solve superhuman driving.”
An interesting comment, as it destroys one thing that HW3 owners were holding to: Tesla was delaying HW3 upgrades until it had AI5. Now, it’s clearly not the case and Tesla has no excuse not to upgrade HW3 cars.
He described AI5 as “a gigantic improvement. Roughly 12X more compute,” and later as “roughly an order of magnitude hardware performance improvement, all things considered. Memory bandwidth is a constraint.” Last year, he said that by some metrics AI5 would be 40 times better than AI4.
AI5 is also moving around. In October, Musk said Tesla cut AI5’s RAM in half to 72GB to get enough volume for Optimus, then nudged it back up to 96GB a day later. AI6 was cut by a third, to 144GB of LPDDR6. When asked about AI6 this weekend, Musk replied with a chef’s kiss meme.
As we reported in July, Samsung’s Texas fab won’t reach AI5 volume production until the second half of 2027 , nearly two years behind Musk’s original timeline. And that volume is now headed to robots and data centers, not cars.
Electrek’s Take
This is the situation for AI4 owners: v15 has to be the one. And we heard Elon Musk calling every FSD update “the one” for the last decade.
Tesla’s own engineers are talking about squeezing the last few percent of utilization out of AI4. Musk describes a half-accelerator scrap of compute left for the visualizer. The AI4.5 refresh is a RAM swap that just got downsized, and AI5 isn’t coming to cars. If v15 can’t get to unsupervised driving on AI4, there’s no hardware escape hatch for the fleet.
We’ve seen this movie before. Tesla said HW3 was enough for unsupervised self-driving until it wasn’t, and those owners are still waiting on an answer about upgrades. AI4 owners paid for the same promise.
And even if v15 drives well, I want to know how Tesla handles a chip failure with nobody behind the wheel. That’s not optional for Level 4. If the stack needs both SoCs to drive, what brings the car to a safe stop when one of them crashes?
As for v15 itself, I’m not drawing conclusions from influencer clips. Reality View looks great, but it’s also visibly laggy, and Musk admits it’s compute-limited. A great visual update is nice. Driving performance is what matters. I’ll wait until I get it in my own car to see how big the improvement actually is.

Ford Targets Certain Japanese Customers With Ranger, F-150, and F-Series Super Duty Pickup Trucks
11 photos
Photo: Ford
Ford intends to push four pickup families onto certain Japanese customers. The Ranger opens the list, followed by the Ranger Super Duty. Higher up the spectrum, the full-size truck segment is represented by the F-150 and F-Series Super Duty, with the latter family stretching from the F-250 to the F-550 workhorse. Ford's global export distributor has appointed Yokohama-based Space Factory as the authorized channel partner in Japan.
Space Factory will bring these vehicles to Japanese government, defense, and humanitarian customers, giving Japanese customers access to a broader Ford truck range than ever before. The Ranger may be perfectly fine over difficult terrain, but an F-550 configured for specialist equipment occupies a very different corner of the market. Ford wants to cover both, and everything in between.
From Japanese ministries to local governments, independent administrative agencies, the Self-Defense Forces, and nongovernmental organizations, there are plenty of prospective customers out there. Their requirements include personnel and equipment transport to remote areas, logistics, disaster relief, and humanitarian operations. Unfortunately, this arrangement is anything but a return to retail sales for the second-largest American automaker after General Motors.
RMA Group-controlled Global Fleet Sales says the Ranger excels over difficult terrain, making it the perfect candidate for organizations that operate in mountainous regions or on remote islands. Being a narrower truck, the mid-sized Ranger is the superior off-road machine in this particular context.
The Super Duty, which wouldn't have been possible without Ford Australia's involvement in the project, is a heavy-duty midsizer developed specifically for clients who need more carrying and towing capacity. Global Fleet Sales lists the Ranger Super Duty with 1,982 kilograms (4,370 pounds) for maximum payload and 4,500 kilograms (9,921 pounds) in terms of maximum towing capacity.
Photo: Ford Australia Those numbers alone make the Ranger Super Duty an interesting pick for agencies that carry specialist equipment. Communications installations, emergency response goodies, and substantial cargo easily eat into the payload capacity of a conventional midsizer. The Super Duty gives clients more headroom while retaining the footprint of a mid-size truck in a country that is widely known for its narrow roads in dense residential and remote mountainous areas.
Stepping up to the F-150 gets you higher payload and towing capacities. In the United States of America, the 2027 model tops 2,440 pounds (1,107 kilograms) and 13,500 pounds (6,124 kilograms), respectively. The big news for 2027 is the canning of the 2.7-liter EcoBoost twin-turbo V6 in favor of the 3.0-liter EcoBoost twin-turbo V6, a mill that produces a bit more power in the Ranger Raptor.
Above the F-150 sits the Super Duty line, covering a variety of applications. The F-450 with dual rear wheels and the Power Stroke diesel is good for up to 40,000 pounds (18,143 kilograms) when properly equipped, whereas the F-350 with dual rear wheels and the Godzilla naturally aspirated V8 gasser is capable of hauling 7,900 pounds (3,583 kilograms). Importing trucks from the US and Thailand won't satisfy all customers, though.
All targeted clients have different requirements, and that's where RMA Special Vehicles of Thailand enters the picture. This company will provide its vehicle engineering expertise to modify the vehicles as required. Its existing portfolio includes a light tactical vehicle derived from the Ranger Super Duty, utility conversions based on the F-350, and an F-550 oil tanker conversion.
To recap, Global Sales Fleet provides the aforementioned trucks, RMA Special Vehicles does the conversion work, and Space Factory handles servicing in Japan. As of this writing, Global Sales Fleet hasn't confirmed any orders in the Japanese market.

The FDA rejected Capricor Therapeutics’ Duchenne muscular dystrophy cell therapy for a second time on Friday, citing data integrity issues. CEO Linda Marbán told BioSpace she was shocked and explains why she thinks this reason is suspect.
Despite all the controversy surrounding Capricor’s Duchenne muscular dystrophy treatment over the past 18 months, the cell therapy’s rejection— announced by Capricor on Friday—came as a “giant shock” to CEO Linda Marbán. In fact, the biotech had been expecting an approval right up until the night before.
“We believe that the FDA took a dislike to the therapeutic when Vinay Prasad was [Center for Biologics Research and Evaluation] head, and that they developed a negative approach to it, and really has never given the therapeutic, the trial, the data, any of it a fair shake,” Marbán told BioSpace on Saturday.
The FDA took the rare step of issuing a public statement about the rejection on its website. Agency reviewers cited “unauthorized” changes made to the pre-specified statistical analysis plan (SAP) and “violations of study blinding procedures” in deramiocel’s Phase 3 HOPE-3 trial. The FDA also flagged “serious clinical trial data integrity deficiencies,” which the agency said “render the study data unreliable and incapable of post hoc remediation.”
The FDA’s concerns stem from an inspection by the agency’s Bioresearch Monitoring (BIMO) Program. But Marbán noted that Capricor commissioned its own audit, by inSeption Group, which showed that the trial data were “never touched, never manipulated.” The biotech sent the group’s findings to the FDA but never received any feedback, Marbán said. She thought those issues had been resolved.
“The fact that they have tried to make this about a data integrity issue suggests that there is something deeply rotten in the state of Denmark,” she added, quoting William Shakespeare’s Hamlet .
The devil is in the details
Capricor and the FDA locked horns during an advisory committee meeting this summer over statistical analysis plans (SAP). For its review, the agency relied on SAP 1.1 as a “benchmark” because it was the plan in place when the study initiated, FDA biostatistical analyst Tingting Zhou said during her presentation.
But Marbán told BioSpace that this version was an unsigned, incomplete internal draft that Capricor never intended to be considered in the approval application. SAP 1.1 became obsolete with the addition of the Phase 3 HOPE-3 trial’s cohort B and did not include content specifically requested by the FDA, she explained. Instead, Capricor based its own conclusions on the most recently submitted SAP 3.0.
Regulatory
Capricor CEO won’t rule out legal action against FDA after negative adcomm
After an FDA advisory committee voted 9-3 on Wednesday against recommending Capricor Therapeutics’ Duchenne muscular dystrophy cardiomyopathy drug for approval, stakeholders allege an “ulterior motive” and “biased intentions.”
July 31, 2026
·
6 min read
·
Heather McKenzie
Read more
Certainly, there have been differing interpretations of the data behind deramiocel. While Capricor claimed in December 2025 that the therapy had met its primary and secondary endpoints, showing statistically significant benefits in upper-limb function and slowed decline in cardiac function as measured by left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), the FDA disagreed in briefing documents issued ahead of the adcomm.
However, earlier this month, an abstract presenting cardiac results from the Phase 3 trial received the American Heart Association’s received Outstanding Research Award in Pediatric Cardiology.
Capricor had originally sought to market deramiocel—which is made up of allogeneic cardiosphere-derived cells— for Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) cardiomyopathy. DMD is a progressive neuromuscular disease primarily affecting boys and young men. It is characterized by muscle weakness, loss of function and respiratory and cardiac complications. Cardiomyopathy is the leading cause of death for patients, who do not typically live far into adulthood.
The discussion at the July 29 adcomm thus primarily focused on the cardiomyopathy results, the HOPE-3 trial’s secondary endpoint. But these data failed to impress the FDA’s advisors, who ultimately voted 9-3 against the therapy’s approval. Capricor then pivoted to an indication of upper limb function, which garnered a more positive discussion at the meeting. The FDA classified this change as a major amendment, pushing the decision date from August 22 to November 22.
This classification raises another red flag in terms of the FDA’s focus on data integrity, Marbán said, recalling a conversation Saturday morning with an investor who asked her, “‘If they [FDA] really questioned the data integrity, why did they grant the major amendment, and why did they have an adcomm to begin with?’”
Marbán also takes issue with the FDA’s communications throughout the regulatory journey for deramiocel. The agency’s new Rare Disease Framework Initiative , intended to provide a regulatory process that is evidence-based but adaptable, includes a commitment to “providing greater clarity, consistency, and predictability in regulatory decision-making through tailored guidance and transparent communication.” This has not been Marbán’s experience over the past two years.
In June 2025, for example, the CEO was blindsided when Prasad unilaterally canceled a previously scheduled advisory committee meeting for deramiocel without giving the company notice. She ended up learning of that development from investors who called her asking what had happened—and she had no answers to give.
And communication did not improve after Prasad left the agency, she added. “We submitted 13 meeting requests between April and October, and zero were granted.”
A path forward?
After two rejections—the first in July 2025—and considerable acrimony between the two parties, is there a path forward for deramiocel?
“FDA approaches rare disease applications with every intention of finding a path forward,” the agency wrote in its statement about deramiocel; “however, flexibility in regulatory approach cannot come at the cost of the foundational requirement that the data underlying an approval decision be reliable.”
The FDA recommended that Capricor conduct another randomized, controlled trial of the therapy, which Marbán said “would probably take about four years to enroll and conduct.”
Capricor will also have to lay off “several hundred people,” the CEO revealed to BioSpace . “So right at the holidays, people are going to be losing their jobs, all because [the FDA] refuses to look at the data the way that everybody else has looked at the data.”
Capricor has already cut around 10% of its workforce , the company revealed in a third quarter earnings report on Nov. 10. The move was made to “to align our organization with our near-term priorities,” Marbán said during an investor call that day. Capricor had 231 full-time employees as of Dec. 31, 2025, according to an SEC filing .

Awaiting a decision on Nov. 22 for its embattled Duchenne muscular dystrophy cell therapy deramiocel, Capricor has reduced its workforce by 10% and slowed programs not directly related to deramiocel, the biotech revealed in its third quarter earnings report.

Outside the U.S., Capricor has submitted applications for deramiocel in Europe and Japan. But Marbán said these applications are going “very slow because we put all of our energy into U.S. and so we’ll start rebooting that in a very active way.”
As for Capricor’s overall status, Marbán said the biotech is still evaluating.
In its press release on Friday, Capricor announced a conference call on Monday morning. That call has now been postponed to a yet-to-be-disclosed date and time.
“Given the significance of these matters, the company is taking the time to prepare an update for shareholders and the Duchenne community on its response to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration’s (FDA) Complete Response Letter for deramiocel and its next steps,” the biotech said in a Monday update.
Capricor shares were trading at $1.91 premarket on Monday—a nearly 75% drop from Friday’s close of $7.59 per share.
“We’re in good shape financially,” Marbán told BioSpace on Saturday. “We have money to do another trial should we decide that that’s the best path forward, but I’m not sure it is.”

By: Northern Miner Staff November 23, 2026
Kenmare Resources (LSE, ISE: KMR) shares jumped after the Dublin-based miner agreed in principle to be acquired by Abu Dhabi’s International Resources Holding (IRH) in a deal potentially valued at £352.8 million ($461.6 million).
IRH’s proposed 380p a share cash offer is 52% above Friday’s London close of 250p for Kenmare stock. It would give Kenmare an enterprise value of £487.1 million, including net debt, according to a statement dated Monday. IRH is also discussing up to $25 million in interim funding for Kenmare.
Kenmare’s directors were inclined to recommend an offer unanimously if the parties settled the remaining terms, according to the statement. No firm offer has been announced.
“The Kenmare board also considers IRH would be an appropriate owner of Kenmare for the next stage of its growth and development,” Kenmare said in Monday’s statement.
Kenmare shares jumped 20% to 299p Monday afternoon in London, valuing the company at about £339 million. They’ve traded between 247p and 338.88p in the past year.
Dividend halt
Weak mineral sands prices have squeezed Kenmare’s cash flow and prompted it to suspend dividends. Without interim funding from the bidder, the company expects it would need to raise at least $50 million in equity before expenses in early 2027. It’s already discussing changes to its revolving credit agreement with lenders.
Kenmare’s key asset is the Moma titanium minerals mine in Mozambique.
Preconditions to the transaction include Mozambican change-of-control consents and completion of outstanding administrative steps for an addendum to Moma’s implementation agreement with the government.
IRH must also receive confirmation of any Mozambican non-resident capital gains tax liability arising from the acquisition and be satisfied with the amount. Other requirements include shareholder commitments and definitive transaction documents. The conditions may be waived by the bidder, which has until 5 p.m. Dublin time on Dec. 15 to announce a firm offer or withdraw, unless the Irish Takeover Panel extends the deadline.
African portfolio
At Moma, Kenmare produced 233,600 tonnes of ilmenite in the quarter to Sept. 30, 12% more than a year earlier. Delays commissioning Wet Concentrator Plant A nevertheless led Kenmare to cut its 2026 forecast on Oct. 15 to 710,000–750,000 tonnes from about 800,000 tonnes. Ilmenite supplies titanium dioxide used in white pigment.
Acquiring Kenmare would expand the bidder’s existing African mining portfolio into mineral sands. IRH, a subsidiary of Abu Dhabi-listed Two Point Zero Group, already holds majority interests in Mopani Copper Mines and Alphamin Resources.
Moma supplies about 6% of global titanium feedstocks, according to Kenmare, and also produces zircon. Kenmare expects Plant A to consistently achieve its nameplate capacity in the first half of 2027, making the commissioning programme a key operating milestone.
Kenmare is also studying whether to recover more value from Moma’s monazite, a mineral containing rare earth elements. It completed a prefeasibility study in the third quarter and is advancing to a definitive feasibility study alongside discussions with potential buyers.

You guys already know I'm a big believer in buying used Z06s of the C8 variety, especially now that prices have come down considerably compared to what people were paying a few years ago. However, there are a few things I wouldn't compromise on when it comes to supercars, and accident history is definitely one of them.
Take this 2023 Z06 Coupe 3LZ for instance - recently up for grabs at auction where the bidding stopped at $85,000, falling short of the reserve. The seller called the result "close", which means they were probably expecting around $90,000? At least, that would be my guess.
But here's the thing. Not only does this car have 24,000 miles on the odometer, it also has a "dirty" Carfax report, which lists damage to the front, left side, and left front corner. It's tough to gauge the full extent of the damage, and not even the selling dealer could provide us with all the necessary details. Here's what they had to say in the ad's comments section:
"We do not know exactly what happened during the accident. The car looks perfect! We have tried calling Selman Chevrolet to get more information but they refuse to provide it. The paint looks original. The bumper doesn't even look like it has been repainted and it is possible that it has not been."
"It is possible that something went through the radiator and condenser which had to be replaced, likely under insurance claim."
To be fair, the car sounds like it's in really good shape, but for $90k? You can find one with a clean Carfax for roughly that sum; maybe a few grand more. So yes, I'd rather pay another $10,000 or so for a clean example - just recently we saw a 2023 Z06 Coupe 2LZ go for $92,500 with just over 5,000 miles on the clock. That's the sweet spot.
As for this particular car, the spec isn't bad, obviously. It's got an Amplify Orange Tintcoat exterior, Jake C8.R graphics (for a motorsport-inspired vibe), LED headlights, a rear spoiler, plus a set of 20" and 21" forged wheels with Michelin tires and ventilated discs at each corner. It also comes with a front-axle lift system and Magnetic Selective Ride Control.
Photo: Bring a Trailer Meanwhile, interior highlights include the Jet Black leather GT2 bucket seats (heated/ventilated/power-adjustable), a 14-speaker Bose sound system, dual-zone automatic climate control, cruise control, the Stealth Interior Trim Package, plus your basic electronic driver aids such as rear cross-traffic alert and blind-spot monitoring.
As for performance, you already know what's up with the 5.5-liter LT6 V8 . It's sending 670 horsepower and 460 lb-ft of torque to the rear wheels via a Tremec TR-9080 eight-speed dual-clutch automatic. This Vette was factory-fitted with a performance exhaust system featuring driver-selectable modes.
So, what do you guys think? Was $85,000 a reasonable offer? I believe that it was. Maybe even generous (depending on the extent of the damage and the quality of the repairs). There's also some curb rash on the right-front wheel, but that's obviously only a minor concern.

BMW’s new iX4 is almost here, and it could make range anxiety a thing of the past. With 428 miles of EPA range, more than 500 miles on the WLTP cycle, and ultra-fast charging, the new EV could make road trips a whole lot easier.
BMW iX4 enters production ahead of March 2027 launch
Series production of the new iX4 is officially underway at BMW Group’s manufacturing plant in Debrecen, Hungary.
The iX4 is the second fully electric BMW model built at the facility, following the record-breaking production ramp-up of the new iX3 SUV.
BMW said the plant began series production of an entirely new model in less than two months after the company introduced a 24-hour, three-shift schedule to ramp up output to meet higher-than-expected demand.
