The new iX4 will go on sale in March 2027 as an all-electric replacement for the X4. It will be available in two variants: the BMW iX4 50 xDrive and BMW iX4 40 xDrive, with a range-topping M60 xDrive set to follow shortly after.
Both versions use a dual-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) powertrain. The iX4 50 xDrive provides a combined 468 hp and 475 lb-ft of torque, enabling it to sprint from 0 to 60 mph in 4.7 seconds.
BMW launches series production of the new iX4 (Source: BMW)
The performance M60 version delivers a combined 603 hp and 645 lb-ft of torque, which BMW says is good for a 0 to 60 mph sprint in just 3.9 seconds.
The iX4 features a distinct coupe-SUV-like silhouette rather than the traditional boxy, upright SUV design of the iX3. With a rakish roofline and an aerodynamic design, the new iX4 has a drag coefficient of just 0.23.
Like the iX3, the iX4 is based on BMW’s Neue Klasse architecture with its sixth-generation (Gen6) eDrive system.
BMW iX4 M60 (left) and 50 xDrive (right) (Source: BMW)
While EPA figures have yet to be finalized, BMW said the new iX4 has an estimated driving range of up to 428 miles on a single charge using a 112.2 kWh battery. Under WLTP conditions, it offers an all-electric range of up to 514 miles (828 km).
Thanks to its 800V architecture, BMW’s new iX4 can add up to 184 miles of range (384 km on the WLTP cycle) in just 10 minutes with charging speeds of up to 400 kW. Charging the vehicle from 10% to 80% takes about 21 minutes.
BMW iX4 interior (Source: BMW)
Like BMW’s other Neue Klasse models, the new iX4 features its updated interior design. The setup includes a large 17.9″ infotainment screen and BMW’s new Panoramic Vision, a 42″ display spanning the base of the windshield.
The iX4 is 188.3″ long, 74.6″ wide, and 63.3″ tall, with a 114.1″ wheelbase, which is about the same size as the iX3. However, it’s slightly lower than the iX3 thanks to the sloped roofline.
Like all Gen6 BMW models, the new iX4 supports bidirectional charging, enabling it to be used as a mobile power source for e-bikes, camping equipment, or other electrical devices.
The new BMW iX4 50 xDrive will go on sale in March 2027, starting at $66,300, or $4,800 more than the iX3 50 xDrive. That doesn’t include the $1,495 destination fee.
In Germany, the new BMW iX4 40 xDrive starts at €70,900 ($77,500), and in the UK it’s priced from £53,250 ($69,500), OTR.

Courier and parcel prices rose 10.2% in the third quarter from a year earlier, and local freight trucking prices rose 10.7%, according to the first edition of GEODIS’ U.S. Final Mile Index . Consumer prices rose 3.5% over the same period.
The index, released Nov. 18, rose 10.5% overall, with double-digit increases on both the parcel side and the truck side of the last leg as shippers head into budget season. The edition also tracks a diesel price that set records in September and second-quarter cargo theft losses that more than doubled.
GEODIS builds the index from two Bureau of Labor Statistics producer price indexes. The couriers and messengers series stands in for B2C and parcel delivery, and the local general freight trucking series covers B2B and big-and-bulky freight. Each series is rebased to its 2019 average and weighted equally, which puts the third-quarter index at 149.8 against a 2019 base of 100.
The report publishes both halves separately so shippers can apply their own mix. The series are not seasonally adjusted, which is why GEODIS leads with the year-over-year change. Parcel shippers also track rates through benchmarks such as the TD Cowen/AFS Freight Index, which follows ground and express parcel pricing.
Local trucking prices fell through the 2023 freight recession and have now passed their 2022 peak, the report said. Parcel and courier prices have risen every year since 2019. Over that span, the combined index is up 49.8%, against 30.8% for consumer prices. September read 152.0, the highest month on record.
“There is a difference in price point from one customer to the next. From a service standpoint, it doesn’t change,” Kevvon Burdette, GEODIS’ senior vice president of business development for transportation, said in the report. “The service has to be consistent and over the top regardless of who the customer is.”
In a survey released in August by last-mile software company FarEye, 88% of delivery operators said delivery costs are growing as fast as revenue or faster . Median last-mile costs rose 12% for a second straight year, the survey found.
“So now it’s probably the new normal that our delivery costs overall are increasing by almost double digits year on year,” FarEye CEO Kushal Nahata said at the company’s Last Mile Leaders America conference in Chicago in August.
Fuel and cargo theft
Retail diesel hit a record $6.529 a gallon for the week of Sept. 21, 74% above a year earlier, according to Energy Information Administration weekly data cited in the report. That average is the benchmark for most fuel surcharges. Fuel was also the top cost pressure in FarEye’s survey, named by 70% of operators.
Theft figures in the report come from Verisk CargoNet’s second-quarter count : 677 thefts, down 26%, with estimated losses that more than doubled to $304.6 million from $135.7 million.
“Thieves are not stealing more loads. They are stealing better ones,” Rob Greene, GEODIS’ executive vice president of transportation, said in the report. “Food moves the fastest, tech is worth the most, and both go missing at the handoff, not on the highway.”
Food, beverage and grocery ranked first among the verticals GEODIS considers most exposed to theft in the last leg of delivery. Household goods and big-and-bulky freight came second, followed by high-tech goods and then personal care and beauty. The ranking combines 2025 and first-half 2026 theft data with the judgment of GEODIS’ transportation leaders and is not a claims disclosure for any customer, the report said. GEODIS pairs each vertical with controls it sells, such as two-person delivery crews, geofenced photo proof of delivery , and a custody record for every handoff.
CargoNet’s third-quarter figures , released Nov. 4 after the report’s Oct. 23 data cutoff, show 547 thefts, down 33%, and losses up 12% to $230.1 million. Food and beverage led all categories, with 94 thefts. Metals ranked second, and GEODIS left them off its list because that theft concentrates on linehaul and job sites.
What retailer fines cost shippers
A shipper with $100 million of goods and 10% of cases late or short would pay $300,000 a year in retailer fines, before redelivery and expedite costs, GEODIS estimated. The estimate uses Walmart’s fine of 3% of the cost of goods on noncompliant cases.
“Retailer fines can be a big number, and a lot of shippers bury them, because they don’t sit well with leadership or the CFO,” Burdette said in the report.
GEODIS forecast for the fourth quarter
The company expects the index to stay above 145 in the fourth quarter as September’s diesel spike reaches fuel surcharges and peak-season surcharges land. Preliminary October producer price data, released Nov. 13, puts the index at about 155.6 by FreightWaves’ calculation using GEODIS’ published method.
Why it matters: Shippers budgeting local truck delivery of furniture, appliances and store freight for 2027 face rates already above their 2022 peak, with fuel surcharges still catching up to September’s diesel record. BLS producer price data out Dec. 15 will show whether the index holds above GEODIS’ 145 forecast.

By Alexander Whiteman
23 November 2026
Underlying growth in African airfreight demand is proving more significant than temporary benefits provided by shippers switching from ocean services, as expanding trade and new cargo flows create longer-term opportunities for the sector, according to Kenya Airways.
The carrier acknowledged to The Loadstar that congestion, geopolitical uncertainty, and unreliable shipping schedules had encouraged some business to move cargo to airfreight, but said this was only one element of a broader increase in demand.
“Some of the recent growth has been linked to temporary market conditions, including supply chain disruptions, seasonal cargo peaks, geopolitical developments, and capacity constraints in competing transport modes,” said a spokesperson.
“However, we do not expect a complete reversal of the growth currently being observed. The more significant development is the emergence of long-term structural growth drivers,” countering claims made by some Loadstar sources.
Kenya Airways identified expanding consumer markets, population growth, urbanisation, industrialisation, and increased regional integration through the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) as factors supporting sustained demand for air cargo.
The strongest demand continued to be for East African perishables, particularly flowers, fresh fruit, and vegetables destined for European markets like Amsterdam, London, Paris, Brussels, and Frankfurt.
“We are also seeing continued growth in pharmaceuticals, courier and express products, e-commerce shipments, high-value cargo, and specialised logistics solutions,” the airline’s spokesperson continued.
Citing increasing demand on Africa-Europe, Africa-Middle East, Africa-Asia, and intra-African trade corridors, the spokesperson noted that Nairobi was positioned as a gateway connecting East, Central, Southern and West Africa with international markets.
E-commerce expansion was also contributing to demand, as shorter delivery expectations encouraged retailers and logistics providers to use air cargo for fulfilment and inventory replenishment.
“Collectively, these trends position African air cargo for continued growth in the years ahead,” the spokesperson noted, highlighting emerging cargo categories, pointing to increased movement of solar panels and related equipment destined for the US.
Historically, much of this traffic moved directly from Asia to the US, but changing trade policies, tariff considerations, and manufacturers’ efforts to diversify sourcing arrangements had created alternative logistics corridors involving East Africa.
Since the middle of the year, these movements have generated significant charter and ad hoc freighter activity through Nairobi and the wider region, according to the carrier, reflecting what has been seen elsewhere in the global supply chain.
The spokesperson said that although some disruption-driven demand could moderate as conditions across competing transport modes normalised, the carrier remained positive about the medium and long-term outlook for African airfreight.
“We see clear evidence of structural growth driven by e-commerce expansion, pharma distribution, perishables exports, regional trade integration, supply chain diversification, and emerging industries,” they added.

Record-Setting 1932 Ford Edelbrock Special Is the Dread of Highboy Roadsters
9 photos
Photo: RM Sotheby's/Robin Adams
There are so many highboy roadsters out there people have gotten pretty used to them by now. They all come with open bodies, they are all (almost) based on Fords, and pack shameless engines under their hoods. Highboys constantly sell at auctions for pretty decent sums that float around $50,000. The one we have here, though, is more than ten times more valuable, and unique.
What you're looking at is officially called a 1932 Ford , but those among us who still have a passion for lake racers of old might know it as the Edelbrock Special. Because yes, it has a direct connection to aftermarket performance parts engineer Vic Edelbrock Sr. and the company whose name almost always pops up when discussing a custom car, truck, or SUV.
The connection goes by the name Bill Likes, a man who many decades ago worked as a machine shop operator for the performance equipment company. Encouraged by Edelbrock himself, Likes set out to build one of the most extreme highboys you'll ever hear about.
Starting from a 1932 Ford chassis fitted with a Ford Model A body, Likes went out to create a vehicle that was the star of the show and the dread of the competition in the Russetta Timing Association (RTA) and the Southern California Timing Association (SCTA) competitions back in the 1950s.
The Edelbrock Special made a tour of lake races (and not only) from 1950 to 1957, impressing the crowds and setting records at El Mirage and Bonneville, for instance. During its life, it set no less than 13 such land speed records.
Responsible for those achievements was, of course, the build's engine, which presently presents itself as an over-bored, de-stroked 259ci Mercury flathead V8 fitted, how else, with Edelbrock heads and an Edelbrock intake. Triple Stromberg carburetors are also on deck to finish the job.
After its final race almost seven decades ago, the Ford entered private ownership, and it presently is part of the Boeckmann Collection, which is going under the hammer at the end of January 2027.
Auction house RM Sotheby's is tasked with selling the beaut, and it estimates that it could fetch as much as $600,000 if the right crowd is in the house. If not, it's a bit of a gamble, as the Ford is listed for sale with no reserve.
Whoever lands themselves this piece of racing history on wheels will also get tons of memorabilia, including trophies, timing slips and placards, historic images, and original invoices.
We're told the car is in tip-top shape thanks to restoration work that brought it back to its 1951 form, now boasting black bodywork over an interior as simple as they get, with bomber seats, Stewart Warner gauges, and a dashboard made of what was once an engine.
We will keep an eye on the 1932 Ford Highboy Roadster Edelbrock Special and get back to you with news of how much it sold for .

Both the M9 Dynamic and Premium are solely available with front-wheel drive, though, and feature three intelligent operating modes: EV Pure Electric, HEV Series, where the gasoline engine only acts as a power generator, and HEV Parallel, where both the gasoline and electric motor work together. With declining sales, annual capacity cuts approaching a million units, and a wave of affordable Chinese competitors entering Western markets, Volkswagen is facing down its own mortality. Rather than fighting it, the company is leaning in and announcing plans to export roughly 300,000 Made-in-China VWs per year by 2030.
American dealers won’t be getting any Made-in-China vehicles (not at first, anyway), but for Mexican, South American, Middle Eastern, African, and Southeast Asian markets, the shift to lower-cost Chinese manufacturing marks a major strategic pivot. In addition to exporting budget-friendly sedans like the Jetta VA3, Volkswagen is also considering a move to adopt Xpeng’s tech stack for up to 75% of its core European lineup .
Does Volkswagen have any other options?
Jetta SUV concept; by FAW-Volkswagen.
The move comes as Volkswagen’s Chinese JVs face a sharp sales decline in their home market, selling just 1.2 million new cars in the first nine months of 2026 (down 35% compared to last year). The financial story is even worse, with last year’s roughly $815 million profit falling to a more than $120 million loss.
“The sharp decline in the overall market in China remains an industry-wide challenge,” said Martin Sander, Volkswagen Group’s sales boss, before adding that VW’s “new, locally developed electric models are beginning to make an impact .”

Add in rising energy costs , continuing software issues, and serious labor disputes with the IG Metall union in Europe , and Volkswagen may not have much choice in the matter – which is why it’s not exactly surprising to see VW consider turning China into an export hub. And that 300,000 number? That may be just the start.
On Volkswagen’s third-quarter results call, CFO Arno Antlitz reportedly called that 300,000 annual export target “conservative,” adding that overseas shipments could help offset the carmaker’s weakening prospects in China.

By Stuart Todd
23 November 2026
An EU cap on imports of Chinese hybrid cars could deal a serious blow to the business of European finished vehicle logistics (FVL) players, given this is one the most dynamic segments of the market at present.
However, while not playing down the impact of a move designed to protect the bloc ’ s incumbent OEMs, the Brussels-based Association of European Vehicle Logistics (ECG remains upbeat on the sector ’ s flexibility and ability to adapt.
The EU plans a cap on imports of Chinese hybrid vehicles of 350,000 units, from 1 December, after Beijing agreed to curb exports in a 16-point trade consensus.
There is provision to increase the cap by 6% annually thereafter.
According to Eurostat, the EU ’ s official data source, in the first eight months of 2026. imports of hybrid cars had surpassed the full-year 2025 volume by 64%, and reached 474,475 units – a 175% year-on-year jump.
“ It ’ s not our role to say how many vehicles should be imported. Our interest is in understanding how measures like this could change vehicle flows and what that would mean for logistics capacity,” ECG executive director Frank Schnelle told The Loadstar .
“ Limiting imports to 350,000 units annually would clearly affect FVL operators that handle a lot of hybrid vehicles from China. But a reduction in such imports would not automatically mean fewer cars being sold in Europe. If overall demand holds up, some of that volume could be replaced by other types of automobiles, including battery electric vehicles from China. or vehicles sourced from other markets.
“ For our members, this could mean a shift in transport routes and where vehicles are handled. Capacity is currently well-used overall. Ocean shipping lines are ordering vessels and vehicle storage areas are being expanded at ports.”
The surge in Chinese hybrid cars into the EU over the past couple of years was largely the result of hefty anti -subsidy tariffs on BEVs from China in October 2024, explained Rico Luman, senior sector economist, transport & logistics, at Dutch bank ING.
“ Basically, Chinese brands shifted their sales efforts to hybrids to sidestep these tariffs ,” he said.
However, the tariffs have done little to stop Chinese EV growth in Europe, and sales have remained resilient despite the duties.
Mr Luman quoted data showing China’s share of European new car sales has continued to grow, reaching 10% for the first nine months of the year, compared with 6% in the corresponding period last year.
“ I would expect (in light of the cap on hybrids) a renewed push for Chinese BEV vehicles. Also, a brand like BYD which plans to start its own production in Szeged, in Hungary, will likely start turning out hybrids for the European market, alongside full-electric vehicles. Others, such as Leapmotor, could do this too.
“ All -in-all, this supports European production and will temper Chinese imports somewhat, but without stalling import growth completely. European FVL players will see a reshaping of trade routes. New production locations and ‘ co – operative ’ locations (between OEMs) will emerge and be scale d up, requiring parts that will need to be sourced from Europe. In a changing market landscape agility will be paramount.”
The latest figures from Europe’s biggest port for finished vehicle traffic, Antwerp-Zeebrugge, showed the Far East, which includes China, accounted for more than 55% of imports – 706,228 units – in the first nine months up 28% year on year.
“ The port is operating at near-maximum capacity, given the huge imports from China, among others, ” a spokesperson added.

Harley-Davidson Red Bullet Is a Private Custom Built on a Factory Custom, Rides on 23-Inch Wheel
31 photos
Photo: Thunderbike
If you want to go for an extreme Harley-Davidson, you can always turn to the CVO Road Glide, a factory custom based on a Grand American Touring bagger that already has a lot going for it. A lot of people make that choice, but few of them have the audacity to have a factory custom CVO customized once more, this time at the hands of a third party.
Yet that's exactly what we have here, a custom built on a custom in the form of something called the Red Bullet. Born in Milwaukee as a CVO Road Glide of unspecified model year, it got transformed once more at the hands of German crew Thunderbike.
These guys are used to significant and over-the-top transformations of Harley motorcycles, but even they seem to admit there's not much they can do to turn this thing into an even more exquisite version of itself.
That's why when looking at the Red Bullet one doesn't immediately notice what sets it apart from the stock CVO Road Glide. Well, maybe there is one thing, and that's the wheel installed at the front.
Normally, Harley ships this model with a 19-inch front piece, but Thunderbike opted to install its own 23-inch option. Not just any such option, but one milled from solid metal, featuring wire spokes and given a shiny black and metallic two-tone look.
The wheel swap brought into play the need to modify a number of other parts, including the clutch fitting, slave cylinder, brake lever, and cover for the master brake cylinder. Thunderbike did all that, and the result is, well, as you see it...
The front wheel is partially shielded from the elements by a matching fender, and it required the installation of longer handlebars and a riser kit, which changes the position of the rider to something different than what the stock motorcycle has to offer.
At the back, Thunderbike kept the original wheel, but it did remove it for a little while to machine it so that it replicates the look of its sister at the opposite side of the bike. Also unchanged is the two-wheeler's engine, the mighty Milwaukee-Eight VVT 121 V-twin, which was only gifted with Dr. Jekyll & Mr. Hyde exhaust components. It's unclear how they affect the engine's power levels.
The paint job is not as spectacular as we're used to from other builds signed by Thunderbike, looking a lot like something Harley offers right off the factory floor. It gets the job done, and that's all that matters.
Thunderbike does not reveal how much the conversion cost to make, but I reckon it's not nearly as expensive as many of the other bikes these guys roll out. For reference, though, I'll tell you that the CVO Road Glide of the 2025 model year presently sells for $45,999.

Photo: Liège Airport
By Alex Lennane
23 November 2026
Airlines have rescheduled flights and moved aircraft to airports in neighbouring countries after a Belgian air traffic control strike disrupted cargo operations at Liège and Brussels, four days before Black Friday.
Liège Airport spokesperson Christian Delcourt told The Loadstar some 70 flights were affected. The airport has yet to say how many were cancelled, retimed, or rerouted, or when it expects affected freight to move.
Flight-tracking data showed Emirates SkyCargo flight EK9989 from Dubai, originally due at Liège, was rerouted to Copenhagen. Maastricht Aachen Airport said it expected to take two cargo flights diverted because of the Belgian strike, but did not identify the airlines or the airports the flights were originally due to serve.
Brussels Airport cancelled all arrivals and departures scheduled between 7am and 9pm local time today, and posted the same notice on its cargo arrivals and departures pages, and advised customers with flights scheduled after 9pm to check with their airlines.
It has yet to publish a freighter tally or a timetable for normal cargo operations to resume.
Today’s walkout, part of a national protest against government austerity measures, is the 11th strike to affect Belgian airspace in 11 months, according to the Board of Airline Representatives in Belgium. Brussels Airlines said it only learned late on Saturday afternoon that controllers would take part, leaving little time to rework Monday’s schedules.
A stoppage on 2 June affected 35 to 40 flights at Liège, with some diverted to Cologne, local broadcaster Qu4tre reported. Liège has yet to identify the airports taking rerouted flights this time.
Elsewhere, Charleroi cancelled flights for the whole day, while Ostend-Bruges is working with airlines to reschedule flights, including three cargo departures and two arrivals.
FedEx warned of possible delays to shipments to, from and within Belgium, and Jersey Post Global Logistics also warned that disruption at Brussels Airport could delay inbound international mail and parcels, while the wider strike could affect collections, processing and deliveries across the country.
Chronopost warned that expected blockages on major roads and in industrial areas could lengthen transit times for shipments to and from Belgium throughout Black Friday week. It said all its Belgian sites would remain open, although collections and deliveries would be disrupted.
The recent US air traffic control outage showed how long capacity can take to recover once flights resume. The FAA lifted its nationwide ground stop on 13 November, after less than five hours, but capacity on international flights out of the US was still about 10% below the previous week’s level over the weekend, according to WorldACD. Expeditors warned that recovery would vary by airline and airport as carriers repositioned aircraft and crews.
The strike falls in one of Liège’s busiest periods for freight, as the airport adjusts to a sharp drop in ecommerce traffic. Liège said small-parcel volumes had fallen 42% after the EU’s €3 duty took effect on 1 July, reducing the number of dedicated ecommerce flights. Aircraft movements fell 6% year on year in the third quarter, while freight tonnage was virtually flat, at 334,467 tonnes.
Stronger exports helped lift total throughput 7.3% year on year, to 1.03m tonnes in the first nine months. Liège singled out pharmaceuticals, data centre equipment, and flowers as supporting July volumes.
Last month it signed an agreement with Brazil’s Viracopos Airport to attract freighter services between Belgium and Brazil.

Federal prosecutors uncovered a written playbook instructing commercial truck drivers to divert shipping containers before customs inspections. The document warned about surveillance, GPS trackers and additional security seals. Investigators connected those instructions to a scheme involving tens of millions of dollars in counterfeit and illegal merchandise. Federal court records detail how the operation allegedly moved shipments through Southern California ports.
The instructions outlined when drivers should abandon unauthorized deliveries and proceed directly to government inspection facilities. Otherwise, they directed trucks toward warehouses where conspirators could remove merchandise before federal authorities examined shipments. Prosecutors identified the document as a standard operating procedure, or SOP. Encrypted communications provided investigators with records of its distribution and subsequent revisions.
Federal authorities arrested Zhe Wang, 40, Eric Ly, 38, and Mildred Estrada, 41, on Nov. 20. Wang lives in La Puente, Ly in Temple City and Estrada in Lake Elsinore, all in California. A nine-count indictment charges each with conspiracy, smuggling and breaking customs seals. All three defendants are innocent until proven guilty.
According to court records, Wang operated a logistics company and received instructions from overseas customers in China. Ly worked for an international shipping business and allegedly recruited drivers through industry connections. Estrada coordinated transportation between port terminals, private warehouses and designated examination facilities. The alleged operation continued from at least July 2024 through July 2025.
Written instructions reveal the operation
Investigators traced the operating procedures to an April 24, 2024, exchange between Wang and Ly. Wang allegedly transmitted a PDF titled “SOP” through an encrypted messaging application. Its contents instructed drivers to check containers for signs of monitoring before proceeding toward unauthorized destinations. The document specifically referenced additional seals, GPS equipment and vehicles potentially following shipments.
The original instructions told drivers to “go to the inspection station directly” when they detected surveillance indicators. Otherwise, the message directed them to “go to warehouse.” Prosecutors identified another version of these procedures in communications dated June 24, 2024. That document reinforced the same contingency involving suspected monitoring or tracking equipment.
Federal authorities require selected containers to travel directly to designated examination stations for customs inspection. Prosecutors contend the defendants instead diverted those shipments to unauthorized warehouses first. Conspirators allegedly removed contraband and attached counterfeit security seals before continuing their deliveries. The trucks then transported those containers to their scheduled examination facilities.
Messages also documented preparations involving counterfeit security devices. On Aug. 30, 2024, Wang allegedly sent Ly a photograph showing a high-security bolt seal. He wrote, “every time I make seal that means job is coming.” Another exchange on Sept. 26 referenced two additional counterfeit seals.
The indictment identifies warehouse destinations in Irwindale and El Monte, both located in Los Angeles County. A separate federal cargo theft case also involved criminals allegedly exploiting legitimate trucking operations to redirect shipments. Prosecutors contend Wang and Ly maintained facilities used to conceal illegally imported goods. Estrada allegedly managed transportation arrangements through delivery orders and dispatch communications. Court records do not identify the trucking companies or individual drivers involved.
Payments and messages trace four shipments
The first documented movement involved container CBHU9047612 at the Port of Long Beach on Sept. 12, 2024. Ly allegedly sent Estrada a delivery-order photograph before arranging transportation. A WhatsApp message identified Irwindale as the shipment’s destination. Investigators traced two Cash App transfers totaling $1,212 for related fees and delivery services.
In January 2025, Estrada reported that another company had already claimed the PierPASS transaction for container XYLU8188185. PierPASS administers traffic mitigation fees that help fund extended terminal operating hours at Southern California ports. Despite the issue, the defendants discussed an unauthorized warehouse in El Monte. Prosecutors contend the shipment stopped there before its scheduled customs inspection in Carson, California.
On June 13, 2025, Ly referenced another delivery order during an encrypted conversation with Estrada. She responded, “dispatching driver right now to pull out.” The indictment describes an unauthorized diversion involving container FFAU6047760. Investigators identified a $1,800 Zelle transfer connected to that movement.
The final identified shipment involved container UETU5496981 at the Port of Long Beach in July 2025. Estrada allegedly arranged its collection before customs officers could examine the merchandise. Prosecutors contend participants removed contraband and installed a fraudulent security seal. Ly subsequently transferred another $1,800 through Zelle for the diversion.
The indictment describes payments substantially above normal trucking fees. However, prosecutors do not specify how much the individual drivers received. Other freight fraud investigations have involved legitimate truck drivers who unknowingly followed instructions from criminals controlling shipment arrangements. Investigators identified communications involving delivery orders, container identifiers and warehouse instructions. Those records form part of the government’s account of the alleged conspiracy.
Federal charges and unresolved details
The indictment contains one conspiracy count, four smuggling charges and four offenses involving customs seals. Each defendant faces a statutory maximum of 20 years for every smuggling conviction. Breaking those security devices carries up to 10 years per count, while conspiracy carries five. Homeland Security Investigations and the Environmental Protection Agency Criminal Investigation Division are investigating the case.
The filing describes additional participants but does not identify every individual involved. Prosecutors have not named the motor carriers, international shipping company or specific warehouse addresses. The document also omits individual shipment valuations despite describing tens of millions in illegal goods. Court records do not establish whether every participating driver knowingly assisted the operation.
Why it matters
Prosecutors say the defendants used legitimate trucking operations to move illegal merchandise through California ports. The scheme shows how criminals can exploit the movement of shipping containers between port terminals and customs inspection facilities. Even high-security seals cannot protect cargo when conspirators can replace them before inspection.

This 2024 Chevy Corvette Z06 Coupe Failed To Sell for $94,500 and It's a Lot of Car for the Money
23 photos
Photo: Bring a Trailer
I'm genuinely surprised this Z06 Coupe didn't sell at auction recently. Bidding reached $94,500, which apparently wasn't enough to bridge the gap for the seller, a dealer our of Buffalo, New York. Look, I can certainly understand wanting more money for a low-mileage 3LZ (2,700 miles), but I'm not entirely sure this is a six-figure car, given where the market is right now on used C8s.
Personally, I believe that whoever placed that final bid was getting ready to make an excellent purchase. I mean, the spec is solid and the Carfax is clean. Maybe this wouldn't have been my ideal Z06 spec (because I'm not particularly fond of Torch Red), but I also know that a lot of people love this color and that's perfectly fine.
Oh, what am I even saying?! Having a red Z06 isn't the end of the world. You can always wrap it if you hate the colorway. And there are plenty of contrasting elements on this car to offset all that... red.
You get a carbon fiber front splitter, rear spoiler, LED headlights, and two removable roof panels included in the sale - one is transparent, while the other one matches the body color. That's actually a nice combo to have. I'd definitely use the transparent version more, because again, it increases the contrast.
As for the forged aluminum black-finished wheels, they measure 20" at the front and 21" at the rear, and come with Michelin rubber and Brembo discs. There's also a front-axle lift system with memory settings, as well as Magnetic Selective Ride Control. You know that lift system is pretty much essential on a car like this , especially if you're planning on driving it regularly.
Meanwhile, the interior is exactly what you'd expect from a well-equipped 3LZ, meaning you've got the Jet Black upholstery, heated and ventilated GT2 bucket seats, red seat belts, microsuede upper trim, a carbon fiber and microsuede steering wheel with carbon shift paddles, a head-up display, a Bose sound system, the Stealth Interior Trim Package, a performance data and video recorder, dual-zone automatic climate control, cruise control, and plenty of electronic driver aids.
Photo: Bring a Trailer Underneath all that is Chevy's awesome 5.5-liter naturally aspirated LT6 V8 engine, producing 670 horsepower and 460 lb-ft of torque. Everything gets sent to the rear wheels via an eight-speed dual-clutch automatic gearbox. As you can see, this car came factory-fitted with a red-finished intake, which is a nice touch given the red exterior.
So, what do you guys think? Would you have paid more than $94,500 for this car? I think I would have. Maybe just under $100,000 would have hit the spot. Then again, the seller was under no obligation to accept the highest bid. Sadly, this was a missed opportunity for someone to land a very nice Z06 at a very attractive price.

Paid $15K for V-Code Plymouth Superbird in 1991, Went on 5-Year Beans and Rice Diet To Keep It
53 photos
Photo: Facebook/Dale Mathews
You never forget your first yellow Plymouth Superbird, especially when you are a teenager getting dropped off along an Ohio river to go fishing. Long before he even owned a driver's license, Lenoir, North Carolina collector Dale Mathews spotted a Lemon Twist winged Mopar resting beside a rural homestead.
Years later, that unforgettable silhouette resurfaced at a downriver farm, waiting for fate to close the loop. The break arrived inside an unlikely venue: a European auto repair shop where Mathews had taken his wife's car. Staring at a Superbird poster taped to the shop wall, Mathews caught the proprietor's attention and learned the mechanic owned the very car he had admired since boyhood.
It was not for sale, yet Mathews stopped by every month for half a year until financial pressure forced the owner's hand and triggered the phone call Mathews had prayed for. The seller asked $10,000, a stiff sum in 1991 for a rough project, and rival Mopar hunters were already catching wind of the dormant wing car.
Needing extra time to borrow the cash, Mathews boldly offered $12,000 just to lock down the deal. Ironically, he never even craved a winged car; he strictly wanted a 440 Six-Barrel or a 426 Hemi Mopar, openly admitting he would have passed on the Superbird had it carried the standard U-code four-barrel engine.
Photo: YouTube/Muscle in the Mountains Retrieving the Plymouth from its final resting spot inside a chicken coop required blind faith and serious grit. Its steel nose cone sat detached, significant rust had eaten into the body, and someone had severed the brake lines, though the big-block V8 still fired. Knowing this was his sole shot at Six-Barrel royalty, Mathews parked it patiently while restoring and flipping easier Mopars over the years, waiting until the ducks of finances and workshop schedule finally got in a row for a proper rebuild.
Keeping the Superbird proved even harder than finding it. When his son headed off to college in 2008, Mathews planned to liquidate the winged Plymouth to cover tuition, right as the global financial crisis cratered collector car values. Refusing to surrender a lifetime treasure for pennies on the dollar, he kept the car and survived on beans and rice for half a decade, later sidestepping a year-and-a-half trade negotiation involving Bobby Isaac's personal 1970 Dodge Challenger R/T.
Today, that stubborn loyalty gleams in blinding Lemon Twist Yellow, code FY1, capped by the mandatory black Boar Grain vinyl roof designed to conceal unfinished seams around the flush rear window plug. Black Plymouth quarter-panel scripts, Road Runner Superbird wing and nose decals, and a Wheeling Chrysler-Plymouth-Imperial trunk decal honor its Ohio Valley origins.
Photo: YouTube/Muscle in the Mountains Riding on 15-inch Rallye wheels wrapped in Goodyear Polyglas GT F60-15 tires, it packs a 390-horsepower, 490-lb-ft 440 Six-Barrel (395 PS, 664 Nm) paired with a 3-speed TorqueFlite 727 automatic. Inside, the black vinyl bucket-seat cabin and the authentic 1970 Mopar theater hits immediately, complete with a woodgrain Slap Stik center console, round Rallye instrumentation, an AM radio, and the unmistakable Beep Beep steering wheel horn button.
Rather than locking this Concours-recognized trophy inside a climate-controlled tomb, Mathews regularly exercises it across North Carolina two-lanes. He happily budgets an extra 20 minutes at every fuel stop because awestruck onlookers inevitably gather around to share classic car stories.
That magnetic reaction is rich with historical irony, considering the Superbird began as a desperate corporate rescue mission rather than a styling triumph. When sleek Ford Torino Talladegas outran Plymouth's brick-shaped Road Runner on NASCAR superspeedways, Richard Petty stunned Detroit by defecting to Ford for 1969 after Chrysler refused his plea for an aerodynamic racer like the Dodge Daytona.
Photo: Facebook/Dale Mathews Humiliated and defeated (Ford won the 1969 NASCAR title), Plymouth spent 1969 refining lessons learned from Dodge's Charger Daytona in the wind tunnel, determined to bring The King back home. Built on the 1970 Road Runner hardtop structure grafted with modified Dodge Coronet front fenders and hood, the Superbird wore a 19-inch steel nose cone with fiberglass pop-up headlights and a towering 24-inch aluminum rear wing finalized by Creative Industries.
Non-functional plastic front fender scoops masked tire-clearance cutouts required on race cars, while street models retained a generous 7.2 inches of ground clearance. Assembly at Detroit's Lynch Road plant ran only between October 22 and December 15, 1969.
Cleared for NASCAR competition by ACCUS-FIA on January 14, 1970, the one-year-only moniker immediately terrorized stock car racing's fastest ovals. Petty stormed back to Plymouth and claimed 18 victories in 1970, while teammate Pete Hamilton won the Daytona 500 in a Petty Enterprises Superbird.
Photo: Facebook/Dale Mathews Alarmed by speeds nearing 200 mph, NASCAR effectively outlawed winged aero warriors for 1971 by capping their engines at 305 cubic inches (a meager five liters), slamming the door shut on Detroit's wildest homologation chapter after a single unforgettable season.
Showroom buyers, however, largely recoiled from the radical 221-inch street missile. Priced at a hefty $4,298 base sticker as of September 23, 1969—nearly $1,264 above a base Road Runner hardtop—the Superbird came standard with the 375-horsepower 440 Super Commando, TorqueFlite automatic, and front power disc brakes.
Because its heavy aero hardware only paid dividends above 60 mph, standard Road Runners actually outran it in the quarter-mile, forcing frustrated dealers to strip noses and wings off languishing inventory.
Photo: Facebook/Dale Mathews To satisfy NASCAR's tightened 1970 homologation mandate of one car for every two dealerships locate4d in the United States of Automobile, Plymouth had to build a minimum of 1,920 Superbirds. According to Chrysler Historical Society records, the tally rose to 1,935 examples.
Powertrain totals break down to 1,084 base 440 four-barrel cars, 716 optional 440 Six-Barrels, and just 135 range-topping 426 Hemis, split overall between 851 manuals and 1,084 automatics. Narrowing the lens reveals just how elite Mathews' specification truly is. Among the 716 Six-Barrel examples, 308 carried 4-speeds and 408 received automatics, while 440 four-barrels split roughly 466 manuals to 618 automatics.
Hemi cars went 58 manual to 77 autos. Registry estimates across seven official colors place Lemon Twist first at 23%, ahead of Alpine White at 17%, Vitamin C at 16%, Blue Fire and Tor Red at 14% each, Limelight at 11%, and Petty Blue at 5%.
Photo: Facebook/Dale Mathews Half a century later, the market has vindicated both Chrysler's wind-tunnel lunacy and Mathews' refusal to give in to dietary lust in 2008. Clean 440 Six-Barrel Superbirds routinely command quarter-million-dollar or higher at major auctions today, while untouched Hemi variants soar well beyond $500,000.
Ford Dale Mathews, the true payoff sits far beyond spreadsheets: every time that 440 Six-Barrel salvoes to life and that towering yellow wing slices through the breeze, Plymouth's boldest NASCAR legend flies high again. And no one can put a price on that.

By Ian Putzger Americas correspondent
23 November 2026
The cost of final-mile delivery in the US has risen more than 10% over the past year, according to the Final Mile Delivery Index, published by logistics provider Geodis.
It shows cost in Q3 up 10.5% on the same period in 2025, following a 10.6% year-on-year increase in the second quarter –more than three times the inflation rate of consumer prices, 3.2% in Q3, the index’s authors pointed out.
Since 2019 final-mile delivery prices have increased 49.8%, while consumer prices rose 30.8%.
Inflation is hitting both shippers and carriers: the index shows 46% of delivery operators reported costs rising faster than revenue, while 42% reported cost and revenue rising at the same pace.
Not surprisingly, the index identifies fuel as the biggest cost pressure, followed by driver cost and availability, vehicle operating costs, administration, plus compliance, inefficient routing, and drop density.
While driver costs have been impacted by the decimation of the driver pool, due to Washington’s crusade to eliminate non-domiciled drivers and those with insufficient command of English, compliance costs are largely tied to the rise in cargo crime. Although the number of reported incidents actually contracted from a year earlier, losses more than doubled, from about $135.7m in Q2 25 to $304.6m in the same period this year. This development has been attributed to the increased activity of organised crime in the transport sector.
Whereas food, beverages, and groceries emerged as the most-affected sector, in terms of the number of incidents, the hi-tech industry (ranked third by number of incidents) led the rankings in severity of losses from crime. Theft of consumer electronics declined, but hi-tech hardware and crypto mining equipment emerged as top-tier targets for criminals.
While organised crime has brought a higher level of sophistication to the heists on the final mile, the transport industry needs to do better in crime prevention; it has to take accountability and ownership, said Rob Greene, Geodis’s EVP transportation, pointing to instruments that are available to prevent cargo theft.
The higher impact of cargo crime is hitting carriers and brokers in their compliance costs, notably increased insurance premiums, which tend to be higher for high-value types of cargo. Carriers with general liability cover of $100,000-$150,000, let alone the minimum $75,000 cover required by the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Association, are not used by shippers of server racks for AI centres, Mr Greene noted.
Such contracts typically carry rafts of exclusions, such as the use of secure locks, GPS on tractors and trailers, and clauses forbidding stops along the way. Carriers may also be required to run in convoys. These elements, plus the value of servers shipped and the size of the shipment, account for a large range of potential cost outcomes, both in terms of transport charges and insurance premiums, he said.
Insurance costs have been pushed up further by the US Supreme Court’s ruling that brokers can be held liable for negligence in cases where truckers assigned by them cause accidents. This has caused brokers to tighten their requirements for insurance coverage and financial security of the truckers they use.
The travails of the large integrated carriers and their shift away from e-commerce, other than high-margin traffic, reflect the cost pressure on the final mile from crowd-sourced operations using gig drivers. Mr Greene said this did not make the latter model an automatic choice.
While there is evidence suggesting that using gig drivers is more cost-effective per route, when cost of ownership and volume are taken into account, this works out better if they are used as a supplementary option; employed in a dedicated role is an option not as profitable as it was during Covid, he added.
The index cites a survey by FarEye, which suggests 76% of delivery operators prioritise predictable delivery, whereas only 6% view the fastest possible delivery as the top priority. Besides offering a lid on cost, this could also have a positive impact on crime prevention. Mr Greene mentioned that Geodis employees were encouraged to slow down and check if they felt rushed by a potential client or business partner.
Cost will continue to pressure supply chains next year 2027, according to the latest edition of the Supply Chain Navigator, produced by the Kearney Supply Chain Institute. This projects global costs to rise 2.7% or more by Q3 27, and its authors predict a broad range of variation by markets, with inflation in the US potentially as high as 5%, 3.1% in Germany, and 8.3% in India.

After J&J’s $14.6 billion buyout of Intra-Cellular Therapies, the biotech’s former CEO Sharon Mates is still chasing intracellular signaling, this time with Ritzey Therapeutics for metabolic and neurologic diseases.
Ritzey Therapeutics is officially checking in to the biotech scene, raising $112.5 million to advance its pipeline of DYRK1A inhibitors for chronic conditions, including its clinical-stage lead program designed to save and repair cellular function.
The biotech is founded and helmed by Sharon Mates, creator and CEO of neuro-focused Intra-Cellular Therapies, which Johnson & Johnson acquired for $14.6 billion in early 2025—the industry’s biggest deal of that year. Intra-Cellular developed Caplyta, the once-daily oral atypical antipsychotic that now has approvals in schizophrenia, bipolar I or II depression and major depressive disorder.
At Ritzey, Mates is joined by former members of Intra-Cellular’s senior leadership team, though the company didn’t name specific individuals in a Monday press release .
The series A financing was led by life sciences venture capitalist firm Vida Ventures, with participation from Fidelity Management & Research Company and Alexandria Ventures, among others.
The new cash infusion will fuel Ritzey’s pipeline of DYRK1A inhibitors, including its lead candidate, a once-daily oral asset stemming from the recently wrapped acquisition of the French biotech Perha Pharmaceuticals. Ritzey did not disclose financial terms of the buyout.
The lead DYRK1A inhibitor has completed early-stage clinical development, with Ritzey chauffeuring the program into Phase 2 studies. The biotech plans on evaluating the candidate’s effects on pancreatic beta cell function and tau pathology in Down syndrome, plus pancreatic beta cell function for type 1 and type 2 diabetes in the general population.

DYRK1A is a protein kinase on chromosome 21 that regulates cell growth, acting as a “master brake” for pancreatic beta cell expansion and function, as well as for neuronal and inflammatory processes, according to Ritzey.
Individuals with Down syndrome have three copies of chromosome 21, meaning DYRK1A is overexpressed. This contributes to pancreatic beta cell pathology—or insulin insufficiency—and increases pTau, an early predictor of Alzheimer’s disease.
“Our team has a rich history of investigating and understanding intracellular signaling pathways to develop and deliver innovative medicines for the treatment of chronic diseases,” Mates said in a prepared statement. “Bringing that same expertise to Ritzey, we will continue to work towards improving the treatment of chronic diseases for patients.”
She added, “At Ritzey, we have the opportunity to advance a novel mechanism of action that could effectively alter the course of these chronic diseases.”

The AI infrastructure boom is drawing capital at a pace the freight industry has never had to secure. It is also drawing organized crime.
David Warrick, EVP of Enterprise at Overhaul, has spent more than 30 years in supply chain, including two decades at Microsoft running supply chains for the original Xbox and the Nokia acquisition. He retired in 2022 and then joined Overhaul, the global leader in supply chain risk detection, response, and resolution. In a recent conversation, he described a threat landscape shaped by scarcity, scale and old-fashioned deception.
A build-out without precedent
Warrick put the scale in historical terms. The U.S. interstate highway system took 37 years and roughly $650 billion to build, he said. AI infrastructure spending now runs about double that figure every year across the globe, with a high percentage landing in the U.S.
Warrick said the vulnerability in that spending is not the facility itself. “The bright and shiny data center sitting on the hill is not the problem. It’s the dirt road leading to the data center, which is where all of the challenges really are.”
That road now carries far more value than it used to. Warrick said that five years ago, the precious cargo in cargo-theft conversations was smartphones, with a pallet worth about a million dollars. “Now we’re seeing $17 million pallets, $20 million pallets filled with Blackwell chips,” he said, adding that “you’ve now got $100 million truckloads moving across the country.”
Scarcity spreads the risk
The exposure extends well beyond GPUs and memory. Demand has made nearly every component of a data center harder to find, Warrick said. “It’s across all aspects of the build out of the infrastructure: generators, transformers, bus bars, high voltage switchgear, low voltage switchgear.”
When supply is tight, he said, even parts that look like commodities become worth stealing. A secondary market follows, and criminals have noticed. “There’s a big secondary market for them because of this year’s scarcity,” he said.
Handoffs and hijacked carriers
According to Warrick, the weak points are the same ones that have long plagued high-value freight. “Anywhere where there’s a handoff in the supply chain tends to open up a level of weakness.”
What has changed is the sophistication of the people exploiting them. Warrick described groups that buy their way into legitimacy. “These are criminal gangs that have bought legitimate trucking companies and have been running them for some time as a legitimate business, and then started to gain traction on the load boards because people are not paying attention.”
The most common play is the simplest. Warrick described it as “fake paperwork from a driver, a legitimate trucking company who’s been subcontracted twice and then picks up a load, and then just disappears.” He said the fraudulent pickup is the same method already plaguing consumer electronics, beverage and healthcare freight.
More elaborate tactics are in circulation too. “We’ve seen criminals who have quickly resprayed a truck. They’ve changed the DOT numbers. They’ve switched the license plates.” Warrick said thieves have also turned to electronic countermeasures. “We’ve seen them use signal jammers,” he said, noting that much track-and-trace capability depends on truck telemetry and IoT devices placed along roads. In his view, there is “no typical MO in this one.”
Why the economics favor the thief
Warrick framed the threat as industrial rather than opportunistic. “These are transnational organized criminal gangs. Think cartels, right?” He said such groups operate with finance and HR departments and weigh their options accordingly. “A pallet of smartphones for a million dollars, or a pallet with some Blackwell chips on it for $15 million, which are you going to take?”
The goods themselves add to the appeal. Unlike narcotics, chips are legal to hold and move. “It’s easy to ship these things around even across borders because they’re not illegal goods,” Warrick said. He pointed to Russia, Iran and China as destinations of concern, particularly given denied-party screening issues.
Shipper behavior can compound the problem. Warrick said some shippers, wary of building a $100 million truckload, are shifting to smaller vehicles such as transit vans and box trucks. The logic is sound from a transportation standpoint, he said, but criminals see something else. “I can pick up a Sprinter van with a $15 million pallet in the back,” he said, describing how a thief might think about it.
A loss that goes beyond the cargo
For most shippers, the cost of a theft is more than the product itself. Warrick said that outside AI infrastructure, customers tell Overhaul that “the monetary value typically doesn’t even hit in the top four reasons” they worry about. Customer satisfaction, empty shelves and brand damage usually rank higher.
AI infrastructure is different. Warrick said the stolen item is often part of a just-in-time build with no slack in it. “If I lose a specific component, I don’t have an automatic way of being able to replace that because everything’s already been bought and sold for the next number of years.”
That means a theft can delay compute capacity that has already been contracted. “Any disruption to that has a direct monetary impact to the hyperscaler or the neo cloud provider or whoever it is,” Warrick said. He also said many large thefts never become public, partly because “there’s a level of embarrassment around this.” He noted that thefts “into the 10s of millions of dollars” have occurred in recent weeks.
Anatomy of a recovery
Warrick described one recent recovery, without naming the parties. A well-known carrier had subcontracted a load, and the pickup turned out to be fraudulent. Overhaul was tracking the shipment. “We were watching the load. We noticed an unscheduled stop.” The team contacted the driver and the shipper’s side, and the explanations seemed legitimate at first but something felt off.
Overhaul’s analytics flagged the load as well. Warrick said the company has built up a data set from tracking cargo across the industry and is “adding about 200 million data points every month.” When those signals lined up with the human suspicion, the team worked with local law enforcement to intercept the load and recover it. The driver was taken away.
Warrick said the model is about more than alerts. “It’s more than just dots on a map,” he said, adding that “we manage the entire process.” He said Overhaul works closely with local agencies on the ground around the world. “This problem is not getting smaller,” he said.
Deterrence is still a gap
Recovery is only part of the answer, Warrick said. He cautioned that “we’ve got some work to do, even from a legislation perspective,” and said the goal should be “a punishment that sticks” so that future offenders think twice. He said he expects the trend to continue, since more money is flowing into the build-out.
Treat cargo like cash
Warrick’s advice for shippers was to slow down and verify. “If you think about your shipments not as inventory but as cash, you would pay a lot more attention if you had a pallet loaded with dollar bills.”
He said that mindset should translate into process. “It’s okay to take your time, and it’s okay to check and double check.” He encouraged shippers not to hesitate to consult law enforcement or intelligence specialists when something looks wrong, and to treat chain of custody as a front-line control rather than a paperwork exercise.
His final point was about instinct. “If at any point in time something feels off, then just take a breath and actually double check again, because that’s going to be way better than trying to explain $100 million loss.”

LoQus23 Therapeutics is a good match for Eli Lilly’s professed goal of finding biotechs that provide small, early, risky bets.
In Eli Lilly’s 15th deal of the year, England’s LoQus23 Therapeutics will come under the wing of the Indianapolis pharma for up to $725 million, bringing an investigational Huntington’s disease therapy and other assets for triplet repeat expansion diseases.
The cash deal includes an upfront payment and additional milestones, although the specific terms were not disclosed in the Monday morning release .
Lilly has been the busiest pharma of the year on the M&A front. LoQus23 fits nicely into the pharma’s declared pattern of finding small, early-stage bets.
LoQus23 was founded in 2019 with seed financing by SV Health Investors’ Dementia Discovery Fund. The biotech has focused on developing therapies that target DNA mismatch repair, particularly zeroing in on the MSH3 pathway. Later investors include Forbion and the Novartis Venture Fund.

Triplet repeat expansion diseases are genetic disorders caused by abnormal triple repeats in the DNA, leading to protein disruption or other toxic effects in the body. This is a leading cause of neurological and neuromuscular diseases such as Huntington’s and spinocerebellar ataxia type 1 (SCA1).
LoQus23’s lead candidate is LQT-23, an oral MSH3 inhibitor that has shown the ability to block the lengthening of repetitive DNA sequences in Huntington’s during preclinical research. The biotech is working toward a request for human testing of the asset. LoQus23 has not yet declared any other candidates.
Lilly will join a busy but brutal Huntington’s disease space that has seen myriad failures and disappointments. Leading the way to the market is uniQure, which has filed the first-ever genetic treatment for the devastating disease with the FDA. UniQure showed a 75% slowing of disease progression in a Phase 1/2 trial of AMT-130 in September 2025 . But in an update a year later, that improvement lessened , with progression slowing by just 44% after 48 months.

FedEx Corp. has taken a 37% share of InPost, one of the largest European parcel delivery networks, allowing it to make more money from B2C service by tapping strategic parcel locker infrastructure that is less costly than residential delivery while allowing its own network to prioritize higher margin B2B shipments.
On Friday, a consortium of three financial firms and FedEx ( NYSE: FDX ) announced they had completed the buyout of publicly traded InPost, taking it private in a deal valued at $9.2 billion. Advent, a private equity company and previous investor in InPost, also owns 37% of InPost.
InPost is the largest parcel locker operator in Europe and a leader in the rapidly growing out-of-home delivery market that serves e-commerce retailers. It will continue to operate as an independent company under its existing brand.
“Connecting our global network of 3 million businesses and 225 million recipients with InPost’s last-mile capabilities gives both businesses a potential springboard for profitable growth. We see significant opportunity to expand our commercial arrangements across Europe and look forward to building on it as members of the Consortium,” FedEx CEO Raj Subramaniam said in a news release.
InPost, founded in Poland in 1999 by current CEO Rafal Brzoska, has expanded through a series of acquisitions across nine Europe countries where it offers parcel delivery through a network of more than 70,000 parcel machines and 30,000 pick-up and drop-off points, as well as fulfillment services for online merchants and marketplaces. Brzoska retains 16% of InPost through his investment company A&R.
FedEx and its partners said they will accelerate investment in InPost’s pan-European parcel locker network and technological innovations, including its mobile app, to make the delivery experience even more convenient for consumers, which is expected to translate into more orders for merchants.
InPost is well-positioned to benefit from positive market conditions, including increased e-commerce penetration across Europe, rising consumer demand for speed and convenience and the shift towards more sustainable delivery solutions, the consortium said. Using parcel vending machines and retail outlets as delivery and returns hubs requires fewer vehicles on the road and less driving, resulting in less contribution to traffic congestion and carbon emissions. The delivery model is also less expensive for operators because it requires fewer vehicles, drivers and fuel purchases.
Parcel volumes in Europe have quadrupled over five years as consumers increasingly make retail purchases online.
FedEx and InPost will support each other through arm’s length commercial agreements allowing FedEx merchants to connect with InPost’s last-mile capabilities and InPost customers to access FedEx’s vast global network.
“This partnership delivers the long-term capital, global reach and deep technology expertise we require to build on what we have already achieved together as a leading European e-commerce enabler,” said Brzoska. “We’re taking this step with partners who have known InPost for years and understand our business and ambitions.”
InPost last year acquired Yodel for $144 million, making it the third-largest independent parcel operator in the UK, and Spain-based courier Sending. Before that it took over Mondial Relay in France. The carrier’s parcel volumes in 2025 increased 25% to more than 1.4 billion.
InPost also operates in Italy, Portugal, and the Benelux region.
Quarterly results
In the second quarter, InPost revenue grew 18.2% year over year to $1.1 billion on a 16% gain in parcel volume. The carrier handled 381 million parcels in total.
Results were more mixed than in prior periods. The company kept expanding volumes across Poland, the Eurozone and the U.K., and it continued to gain share in locker-based delivery. At the same time, profits came under pressure from higher depreciation, foreign-exchange effects, financing costs and the cost of integrating and scaling its international operations.
Growth was strongest in the Eurozone (up 30%), with UK volume up 16% and Poland up 9.5%, driven by a partial reversal to more front-door delivery. Earnings before interest and taxes declined 18% to $79 million.
Executives said they plan to install about 19,000 additional automated parcel machines this year and expect $532 million in capital expenditure, with about 60% of it allocated to APM production and deployment.
The company cut its full-year outlook, saying it now expects adjusted EBITDA to decline by mid-single digits year over year vs. flat previously, with lower capex and net leverage higher than in 2025.

C.H. Robinson has responded to the lawsuit by several carriers that it had engaged in activity that violates the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act (RICO), at one point describing some of the charges against it as “non-actionable puffery.”
The response filed by C.H. Robinson (NASDAQ: CHRW) Friday in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Texas wasn’t quite as pointed as that of fellow 3PL TQL, also a defendant in the case. TQL, the second-largest broker behind C.H. Robinson, went so far as to essentially say the carriers suing the two companies were not particularly accomplished business operators.
Although it is inevitable the two companies in the case would be seen as a pair of linked defendants. TQL only gets two mentions in passing in the C.H. Robinson response.
C.H. Robinson’ response also contained a request to dismiss the case, citing several reasons. Among them: “Plaintiffs fail to plead the elements that every RICO claim requires: a RICO enterprise and a pattern of racketeering activity.”
The lawsuit was filed in September by a group of carriers, with Stevens Trucking Co. as the lead named plaintiff. It alleges a pattern of “racketeering” by C.H. Robinson and TQL that the carriers say led to them losing business to the two brokers, in part because the carriers say the C.H. Robinson and TQL use “forced labor” that provides them with a significantly lower labor cost.
Specifically, the lawsuit cites freight moved by controversial carrier Super Ego , which was the subject of a 60 Minutes report in April.
Back to the Land of 10,000 Lakes?
In a separate filing, C.H. Robinson asked for the legal action against it to be moved to the U.S. District Court for Minnesota–where it is based–and away from Texas. It notes that none of the plaintiff companies are from Texas.
It also asks for the actions against TQL and C.H. Robinson be severed, because “a single action risks prejudice to both C.H. Robinson and TQL. ”
The C.H. Robinson response, while rebutting the carriers’ points, quickly discusses a longer-term impact from the case that it described as a “troubling phenomenon.”
“Facing financial pressure from the high costs of operating as asset-based carriers and from
the rise of brokerage-based third-party logistics models, plaintiffs look to the RICO statute and C.H. Robinson to compensate them for ordinary business losses in the highly competitive long haul freight market,” C.H. Robinson said in its response.
The Stevens case is an example, according to C.H. Robinson, of what a court warned in a decision in 2019. “For forty years, courts have warned that civil RICO is profligately used as a ‘weapon against legitimate businessmen in ordinary commercial disputes,'” the filing said, quoting a precedent.
In its request for a dismissal, C.H. Robinson raises four key points.
It says the carriers that brought the suit do not have standing for a RICO claim because their complaint “fails to plausibly allege that any of C.H. Robinson’s conduct was either the but-for proximate cause” of their injuries.
Two, the carriers “fail to plead the elements that every RICO claim requires: a RICO enterprise and a pattern of racketeering activity.”
“The Complaint does not plead an enterprise because its allegations merely establish that C.H. Robinson operates a freight brokerage business that contracts with carriers in arm
length commercial transactions, not that C.H. Robinson and these carriers function as a continuing unit,” the C.H. Robinson response says.
The third point is that even if the carriers had been able to prove the first two points, they “identify no racketeering income invested in an enterprise, no injury resulting from C.H. Robinson’s acquisition of an interest in or control of an enterprise, no facts about C.H. Robinson’s participation in and supervision of an enterprise’s affairs and no agreement to violate RICO.”
Lanham Act defense
The fourth summary point is about the carriers’ allegation that C.H. Robinson and TQL violated the Lanham Act, which is where the C.H. Robinson filing makes the “puffery” accusation.
(Puffery is an actual legal term , not just a colorful jibe by C.H. Robinson at the carriers.)
While the 1946 Lanham Act mostly deals with trademark regulations, there also are provisions in the act that, as the C.H. Robinson response says, “prohibit false advertising.”
That charge from the plaintiffs is that C.H. Robinson (and TQL) regularly said they could move freight cheaper and safer than their competitors.
“But none of these allegations identifies (a) the exact language of any such representation or promise; (b) which representations or promises were made to which of the customers Plaintiffs claim (without any factual support) relied on them; or (c) when these representations or promises were made, all preventing C.H. Robinson from being able to respond and the Court from being able to determine whether any particular statement was false or misleading,” C.H. Robinson said in its filing.
Chief legal officer offers comments
Concurrent with its filing, Dorothy Capers, the chief legal officer for C.H. Robinson, described the allegations in the carriers’ lawsuit was a “false characterization of C.H. Robinson and our business practices, and its fundamental inaccuracies about how the freight market actually works.”
“We’ve worked hard to build a network of carriers, from the largest to the smallest, including family-run operations who’ve been hauling freight for our customers for decades and grown their businesses across generations,” Capers said in a prepared statement. “All the carriers we work with are authorized by the federal government, plus meet additional safety standards and higher levels of insurance than legally required.”
The carriers’ lawsuit charges C.H. Robinson and TQL with using its market position and “forced labor” to drive down rates that made it unprofitable for the plaintiffs to operate. “No freight broker sets rates,” Capers said. “The marketplace does.”
Capers added that it is “a myth that freight brokers merely find the lowest-priced carrier. The choice of a carrier for any shipment rides on a multitude of factors.”
With Super Ego having become a toxic company in the trucking industry, C.H. Robinson’s brief response to the specific allegations about its relationship with the rogue carrier is notable if not particularly surprising.
“Plaintiffs include extensive allegations about Super Ego’s alleged safety and labor violations, but nowhere allege that C.H. Robinson relied on Super Ego to haul one of the loads that plaintiffs purportedly lost to C.H. Robinson,” the 3PL’s response said. “That is not enough to establish a direct causal relationship between Super Ego’s alleged misconduct, C.H. Robinson’s bidding on a specific job, and one of the Plaintiffs losing that job.”
The case’s calendar doesn’t put jury selection, if it gets that far, to begin for more than 16 months.

By Bangladesh correspondent
23 November 2026
Bangladeshi garment exporters are turning to costly airfreight to meet delivery deadlines, after weeks of labour unrest disrupted production.
The Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) said on Sunday buyers had shifted confirmed orders for 59 million garments, worth $254m, to other countries.
The association put production losses at $428m in free-on-board value, based on a preliminary survey of 317 factories forced to halt production on between one and 16 days this month
More than 600 member factories were affected and the BGMEA warned that losses could rise sharply if the unrest continued, with most export orders at serious risk because factories were struggling to meet delivery deadlines.
Shahedul Islam, BGMEA secretary general, said the unrest had devastated the industry, explaining: “In an effort to retain export orders, factories are being forced to resort to expensive air shipments, offer substantial price discounts, and even face the difficult prospect of outright order cancellations.”
Protests over the minimum wage began in late October. Work stoppages, damage to factories, and road blockades have disrupted production and transport. On Thursday, the Bangladesh Garment Buying House Association estimated the unrest had caused Tk30bn–Tk40bn ($240m–$320m) in economic losses.
Mr Islam added: “The severity of these losses cannot be measured solely in terms of immediate financial figures. An even greater and potentially irreparable blow has been inflicted on the long-term global reputation, reliability, and future prospects of Bangladesh’s garment industry.”
“It is imperative to overcome this critical situation as quickly as possible in the interest of the national economy and the livelihoods of millions of workers.”
Meanwhile, importers using Chittagong port will have more options for storing goods nearby, with MJL Bangladesh adding five warehouses in South Patenga. Each measures 13,500sq ft, and with the existing 20,000sq ft unit, brings the total covered space to 87,500sq ft on a 2ha site.
However, AmeriBangla’s planned US cotton warehouse in Chittagong has been delayed. The facility would allow Bangladesh mills to buy US cotton from local stock. CEO Aswar Rahman told The Loadstar a batch of US cotton had already sold while still at sea and would go directly to buyers’ factories.
“Our cotton is in huge demand as its cost is lower than West African product and nearly beats Brazil’s.”
He said the company would use the warehouse when it began bringing in larger consignments and that he was in talks with US growers to import 423 containers of cotton. He said AmeriBangla aimed to scale up shipments from the US to 1,600 containers, or 32,000 tonnes, a month over the next two years.
Meanwhile, at Dhaka’s Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, the government has assessed sites for two cargo warehouses, one temporary and one permanent, to ease cargo handling bottlenecks.
